What makes an Atlantic City home sale different?

Selling here means dealing with a barrier-island city of about 11 square miles of land where casino tourism, flood maps and a renter-heavy housing stock all affect the price a buyer offers and the pace of closing. Your three realistic paths are a traditional listing, a sale handled by yourself, or an as-is cash purchase.

Whichever you pick, the same local paperwork applies: a smoke and carbon monoxide compliance certificate, any city occupancy or landlord filings tied to the property, and a deed recorded with Atlantic County. The sections below walk through each piece and point to the city or county office that handles it.

How big is Atlantic City and what do local housing numbers look like?

Atlantic City had an estimated 38,787 residents in mid-2025, up slightly from the 38,497 people counted in April 2020, and it covers 10.76 square miles of land. Owners live in only 30.3% of the city's homes, which means rentals make up most of the housing stock.

Those figures describe the whole city, from Ducktown to the Marina District, so a house near the Boardwalk and one in an inland block can sit far apart on price. Ask for recent sold prices on your own street instead of relying on a citywide median.

How does the casino economy shape home sales on Absecon Island?

Casinos set the rhythm of the local economy, and that carries into housing demand. New Jersey voters approved casino gambling in Atlantic City in 1976, and the first casino opened in 1978. The census shows accommodation and food service sales of about $3.79 billion for 2022, the largest line in the city's business totals.

Gross gaming revenue for the nine operating casinos reached $2.79 billion in 2022, as reported on Wikipedia. Four casinos closed in 2014, and Wikipedia also notes that the Atlantic City area had the highest foreclosure rate in the nation in 2019. Expect buyers to ask detailed questions about condition, flood status and rent rolls.

  • Tourism district areas named in state planning include the Marina District, Ducktown, Chelsea, South Inlet, Bader Field and Gardner's Basin.
  • The Boardwalk runs about 4 miles inside city limits, with casino hotels along it.
  • AtlantiCare Regional Medical Center, founded in 1898, runs its Atlantic City campus in town.

Do flood maps change how an Atlantic City house sells?

Yes, because the whole city sits on a barrier island and buyers and lenders look at flood zone status early. Superstorm Sandy struck on October 29, 2012, caused flooding and power outages, and destroyed the northern boardwalk section fronting Absecon Inlet in the South Inlet neighborhood.

The city's website carries a Property Flood Information page, a Flood Insurance Rate Map, links to the FEMA flood map viewer and a floodplain development form. Before you list, look up your lot's flood zone and pull any elevation certificate you have, since a buyer's insurance quote can change their offer.

What inspections and certificates does Atlantic City require?

Atlantic City's Licensing and Inspection division runs occupancy inspections, and its Fire Prevention forms include a Smoke Detector Application and a Smoke Certificate Affidavit. Call the division before you list so you know which certificate your sale needs.

The city publishes a checklist for the certificate of occupancy on a residential rental unit. Inspectors look at both outside and inside conditions, and the list is a useful pre-sale walkthrough even for an owner-occupied house.

  • Outside: trip hazards in curbs and sidewalks, house number, siding, gutters, windows, railings, roof, fence, steps, foundation and high grass.
  • Inside: working deadbolt, smoke detectors on each level within 10 feet of sleeping areas, a 2A10BC fire extinguisher, carbon monoxide detection, GFCI outlets in bathrooms, two outlets per bedroom, working appliances and no leaks.
  • Seasonal items: window screens from May 1 to October 1 and heat at 68 degrees from October 1 to May 1.
  • Utilities must be on and the unit clean at the time of inspection.

What if the house is a rental or short-term rental?

You will need to deal with the city's landlord and rental rules, because Atlantic City has a Landlord Registration form, a Short Term Rental Public Form and a short-term rental complaint hotline. If tenants live in the house, confirm your registration is current ahead of any contract.

The city also lists a Lead Certification form under Licensing and Inspection, with a list of certified lead evaluation contractors. Landlords should ask the department whether a lead certificate is on file for your unit. Give any buyer copies of the leases so they know what they are taking over.

How are the deed and sale fees handled at closing?

Atlantic County Clerk's Office staff review and record every Atlantic City deed, and the main office is at 5901 Main Street in Mays Landing, with a satellite office at 1333 Atlantic Avenue in Atlantic City. The clerk's recording page says checks for recording and realty transfer fees go to the Atlantic County Clerk's Office, while Gross Income Tax checks go to the State of NJ Division of Taxation.

New Jersey puts the realty transfer fee on the seller. For a sale of $350,000 or less, the state schedule runs $2.00 per $500 up to $150,000, $3.35 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 per $500 from $200,000 to $350,000. With homes in the city valued around $207,400, many local deals fall into that lower schedule.

Sellers who live outside New Jersey file a GIT/REP form, and the state sets a minimum prepayment of 2% of the consideration shown in the deed. Your closing agent usually handles those filings.

Which sale route fits an Atlantic City house best?

Your best route turns on the house's condition, your timeline and how much prep you want to take on. Listing with an agent can reach more buyers but usually means repairs, showings and a lender's appraisal and inspection timeline.

A cash buyer purchasing as-is can skip the repair list, though the city certificate, deed recording and fee steps above still apply. If foreclosure, back taxes or a tenant problem is driving the sale, compare the written terms of every option, including who pays the transfer fee and whether any certificate work falls on you. The city's website also lists a First Time Homebuyer Program, which can matter if your likely buyer is a local household.

More questions about Atlantic City, NJ

Does Atlantic City require an inspection before I sell?

Ask Licensing and Inspection before listing, since the city issues occupancy permits and runs the smoke certificate process through Fire Prevention. Its published checklist covers smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, outlets, heat and exterior condition, so fixing those items in advance avoids delays.

Who pays the realty transfer fee on an Atlantic City sale?

The seller pays it. The state sets the rate per $500 of consideration, and the clerk takes payment at the counter once the deed is filed.

Where do I record the deed for an Atlantic City house?

Deeds go to the Atlantic County Clerk, whose main recording office is on Main Street in Mays Landing. A satellite office operates on Atlantic Avenue in Atlantic City.

Can I sell an Atlantic City house that has tenants or short-term guests?

Yes. Keep landlord registration and any short-term rental paperwork current, and hand the buyer the lease terms. The city has registration forms and a complaint hotline, so open violations are worth clearing first.

Does flood risk change how an Atlantic City house sells?

It can, because the city sits on a barrier island and buyers check flood zones and insurance costs. The city website links to its flood map, FEMA tools and a property flood information page you can review before you list.

What should I know before selling a house in Bayonne?

Bayonne is a dense Hudson County city, with 74,744 residents on a peninsula that has 5.82 square miles of land. A sale there involves a resale certificate through the city, a deed recorded by the Hudson County Register, and for many sellers a look at short-term rental and rent control rules.

This page covers the local numbers, the city steps and the county and state filings, so you can decide whether to list, sell on your own or accept an as-is cash purchase.

What does Bayonne look like on paper?

Bayonne sits on Bergen Neck, a peninsula bounded by Newark Bay, the Kill Van Kull and Upper New York Bay, and it borders Jersey City to the north. The 2020 census counted 71,686 people, up 13.7% from 63,024 in 2010, and the Census Bureau estimates 74,744 for mid-2025.

With about 36% of homes owner-occupied, two- and three-family houses and condos are a large part of the market, and landlords are common sellers. The median home value of $460,100 also sets the price range most buyers will compare against.

How does Bayonne's history and economy affect sellers?

Bayonne was set off as a township in 1861 and reincorporated as a city in 1869, uniting Bergen Point, Constable Hook, Centreville, Pamrapo and Saltersville. Manufacturing, distribution and maritime work still anchor the economy, and part of the Port of New York and New Jersey lies in the city at Port Jersey.

The Cape Liberty Cruise Port sits at the end of the peninsula on the former Military Ocean Terminal, where The Peninsula at Bayonne Harbor now has housing and businesses. Bayonne Medical Center anchors the Broadway shopping district and is the city's largest employer, with more than 1,200 employees. Census retail sales for 2022 reached about $849 million, and transportation and warehousing receipts topped $520 million.

Which roads, rail and schools shape Bayonne home values?

Commuters rely on the Hudson-Bergen Light Rail, which has four Bayonne stops at 45th Street, 34th Street, 22nd Street and 8th Street, and on the Newark Bay Extension of the New Jersey Turnpike (Interstate 78). The Bayonne Bridge, which opened in 1931 and was raised between 2013 and 2019, links the city to Staten Island.

The Bayonne School District serves pre-kindergarten through twelfth grade with 13 schools and 10,059 students in 2020-21, according to Wikipedia. Parks matter to buyers too, including the Hackensack RiverWalk at Collins Park and the Stephen R. Gregg Hudson County Park.

  • The light rail connects Bayonne with Jersey City and its neighbors, and with PATH stations and ferry terminals.
  • The Route 440 retail corridor includes Bayonne Crossing.
  • Average travel time to work is 33.7 minutes, so listings near transit tend to note it.

What resale certificate does Bayonne require?

Bayonne requires a resale certificate whenever a building is sold, and a May 2026 city notice moved that process to the Fire Prevention Bureau at City Hall. Applicants pick up the application from the Fire Prevention office, complete the inspection, and the Fire Department issues the certificate for the sale.

This replaced an earlier arrangement. On October 1, 2025, the Building Department stopped issuing Continuing Certificates of Occupancy and began issuing Resale Certificates for one-family, two-family and multi-family dwellings and commercial buildings. The city said at the time that only the name changed and that the application was shorter. Because the office handling it moved again in 2026, call the Fire Prevention Bureau before you schedule closing. The September 2025 notice listed Building Department lines at 201-858-6334 and 201-858-6073 for certificate questions, which may also help with permit history on the property.

Can I sell a Bayonne house that has been a short-term rental?

Yes, but the city's short-term rental ordinance sets rules that a buyer will want proof of. Under Chapter 33, a short-term rental is occupancy of 60 consecutive days or fewer, and only a property owner can hold the license.

  • Applications go through the city's Spatial Data Logic online portal.
  • Fire safety, building and zoning inspections come first, and the city says a license follows within 30 calendar days of satisfactory inspections.
  • Applicants show no outstanding taxes or water and sewer charges, prior code violations abated and open construction permits closed.
  • A zoning determination letter costs $50 and is requested from the zoning officer at City Hall.
  • A tenant cannot hold the license.

The city website also lists a Rent Control board and a Small Landlord Emergency Grant Program page. If your building has tenants, ask the Planning, Zoning and Development office whether rent control covers it.

Who handles the deed and the state filings in Bayonne?

Bayonne is in Hudson County, so the deed is recorded by the Hudson County Register of Deeds and Mortgages, which lists a phone number of 201-395-4760 on the county directory. Sellers pay the state realty transfer fee. For sales over $350,000, the schedule starts at $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000 and rises to $4.80 per $500 between $200,000 and $550,000.

If you own a Bayonne house but live outside New Jersey, the state requires a GIT/REP form with the deed. Nonresident sellers prepay the larger of 10.75% of their gain or 2% of the deed consideration, so a landlord with a rental in Bayonne should ask the closing agent to calculate the payment before the day of settlement.

Should I list, sell myself, or take a cash offer in Bayonne?

Compare the three on time, cost and risk, using written numbers from each buyer or agent. A cash purchase as-is can avoid repair work and showings, while a listing may reach more buyers on a $460,100 median market.

Whichever way you go, schedule the resale inspection early, since the certificate gates the closing. Mortgage payoff, tax bills and any water and sewer balance come off the proceeds at settlement, and the city lists online payment pages for taxes and water and sewer so you can pull current balances. The same site links an Emergency Rescue Mortgage Assistance page, which is worth reading if missed payments are pushing you to sell.

More questions about Bayonne, NJ

What is the Bayonne resale certificate?

It is the certificate the city requires whenever a building is sold. As of the city's May 2026 notice, the Fire Prevention Bureau at City Hall issues it after an inspection.

Did Bayonne get rid of the continuing certificate of occupancy?

Yes. The Building Department replaced the CCO with a Resale Certificate on October 1, 2025, and the city described the change as a rename with a shorter application.

Where is a Bayonne deed recorded?

The Hudson County Register of Deeds and Mortgages records it. The county directory lists that office at 201-395-4760.

Can I sell a Bayonne property that I rent short term?

Yes. The city's Chapter 33 ordinance limits short-term rentals to 60 days or fewer and requires an owner license with inspections, so confirm your license status before you sign a contract.

Do out-of-state owners owe tax when selling in Bayonne?

They owe a prepayment with the GIT/REP form. The minimum is 2% of the consideration shown on the deed, and the state formula can produce a higher amount based on the gain.

How can you sell a house fast in Bridgeton, NJ?

A cash purchase is the quickest exit in Bridgeton, since no lender appraisal or repair haggling slows it down. Listing opens the door to more buyers but adds showings, inspections and the city's resale form. A sale without an agent lands between the two and carries the same certificate and recording work.

Bridgeton packs a lot of people into a small footprint. Census Bureau QuickFacts put the 2025 estimate at 28,307, up 4.0% over the 2020 base. With only 6.23 square miles of land, the 2020 density was about 4,377 people per square mile, and most blocks mix single-family houses, doubles and small rentals.

What is the Bridgeton housing market like?

Bridgeton is a renter-heavy city with modest values. The 2020-2024 survey period shows owner-occupied homes at a median $145,500, rent at $1,340, and only 36.4% of the 7,481 households owning. Median household income is $55,781, and the average household has 3.21 people, larger than in most New Jersey cities. Those numbers explain why many sellers here are landlords or heirs rather than long-term single-family owners.

The city sits on the tidal Cohansey River near the center of the Delaware Bay lowlands and is the Cumberland County seat. It divides into three sections: Northside, Southside and Hillside. Philadelphia is about an hour away, Wilmington about 50 minutes, and Atlantic City and Cape May roughly an hour. That mix of a low entry price and a reachable job market draws investors, which is one reason cash offers are common.

  • Victorian and Federal-era houses near the downtown core often need roof, porch and plumbing work.
  • Many blocks of "doubles" were built as working-class housing and are now often rentals.
  • Occupied rentals can be sold with tenants in place, but the buyer will ask for the rental registration and inspection record.

Does Bridgeton's historic district affect a sale?

For a large share of the city it can. The Bridgeton Historic District covers about a quarter of Bridgeton and includes more than 2,000 properties ranging from early Federal buildings to 1920s construction. Listed on the federal register of historic sites in 1982, it is described as the biggest district of its kind inside any New Jersey municipality.

If your house is inside the district, ask the city's Historic District Administrative Officer, who works alongside Code Enforcement, what review applies to exterior work before you replace windows, siding or porches ahead of a sale. Buyers who plan renovations will ask the same question. Notable landmarks nearby include Potter's Tavern (built about 1750), the 1795 Old Broad Street Presbyterian Church, and the 1816 Cumberland National Bank building that is now part of the library.

What work and schools shape buyer interest in Bridgeton?

Bridgeton's economy has moved from glass, textiles and iron to agriculture, food processing, health care and public employers. Ardagh Group runs one of the state's larger glass plants in the city, South Woods State Prison (opened 1997) is the largest state prison and a large employer, and the Rutgers Food Innovation Center helps startup food makers. The city lost its remaining glass and textile factory jobs in the 1980s, and farm work continues to draw workers from Mexico and Guatemala; Census data show 54.8% of residents speak a language other than English at home.

Bridgeton Public Schools runs eight schools for pre-kindergarten through grade 12 and had 6,313 students in 2020-21. Schools include Broad Street, Buckshutem Road, Cherry Street, Indian Avenue, Quarter Mile Lane and West Avenue, plus Bridgeton High School. The district is one of the former Abbott districts the state now funds for school construction. Students can also apply to the Cumberland County Technical Education Center in Millville. For getting around, Routes 49 and 77 and County Route 552 are the main roads, and NJ Transit's 410 bus runs between Bridgeton and Philadelphia.

What does Bridgeton require when a house is sold or rented out?

Bridgeton's Code Enforcement Office enforces the 2015 International Property Maintenance Code and also handles home sales. Its page states that on the sale of any property in the city, a resale Certificate of Property Compliance (CPC) form must be filled out and filed with the office. Ask the office about inspection timing early, because a failed inspection means a notice, repairs and a re-inspection before a certificate issues. The Housing and Code department is at 181 E. Commerce Street.

Landlords carry extra steps. Every rental unit must be registered each year by March 1, whether vacant or occupied, and must pass inspection before tenants move in or whenever occupancy changes. The city also adopted a rent leveling ordinance, Ordinance 25-28, which matters to anyone buying or selling an occupied building. Tree removal above set trunk sizes needs an application too.

How do Bridgeton property taxes work for a seller?

Bridgeton's tax load is heavy relative to its home values, which is a common reason owners want out. The assessor's page shows a 2023 total of $5.075 for each $100 of assessed value, built from county ($1.222), county health ($0.068), open space ($0.013), school district ($0.751), municipal ($2.979) and library ($0.042) pieces. Ask the tax collector for the current rate before you quote a monthly carrying cost to a buyer.

The tax collector bills property tax in four installments due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. The same office collects water, sewer and the solid waste charge, listed at $150 for residents and $90 for seniors. Unpaid balances can attach to the sale, so ask for a payoff or statement before closing.

  • Assessment appeals go to the Cumberland County Board of Taxation, 2475 S. Delsea Drive, Vineland, (856) 453-7425, by April 1 or 45 days after notices are mailed, whichever is later, or May 1 after a municipal-wide revaluation.
  • Assessments above $1,000,000 may be filed directly with the State Tax Court.
  • Senior, disabled and veteran deductions are $250 each and require an application to the assessor.

What costs and exemptions does New Jersey apply to an inherited or family sale?

Many Bridgeton sales involve an estate or a relative, and New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee has exemptions that fit those cases. According to the Division of Taxation, the fee does not apply to a deed between a parent and child, between spouses, from an executor or administrator to an heir under a will or intestacy, or recorded within 90 days after a divorce decree. A seller claiming an exemption files Form RTF-1 with the deed.

An ordinary sale is different: the seller owes the fee at recording, calculated per $500 of consideration. On a sale of $150,000 or less, the schedule for deals not over $350,000 is $2.00 per $500, so the fee on a typical Bridgeton price is modest compared with the repair cost of an older house. The Division of Taxation publishes the full schedule.

More questions about Bridgeton, NJ

Do I need an inspection to sell my house in Bridgeton?

The city requires a resale Certificate of Property Compliance form to be filed with Code Enforcement on the sale of any property. Call the Housing and Code department at 856-455-3230 to schedule and ask what the inspector checks.

Can I sell a Bridgeton house with tenants in it?

Yes. Keep the unit registered (due each March 1) and have the current Certificate of Property Compliance and rent records ready, because the buyer takes the property subject to the city's rent leveling ordinance.

How much is the annual rental registration in Bridgeton?

It costs $45 per unit if filed by March 1 and $75 per unit after that date. The registration renewal also covers the rental certificate fees.

Where do I appeal my Bridgeton tax assessment?

Appeal to the Cumberland County Board of Taxation in Vineland at (856) 453-7425, by April 1 or 45 days from the mailing of notices, whichever is later. Properties assessed over $1,000,000 can go straight to the State Tax Court.

Is the realty transfer fee owed if I inherited the house and sell it?

The fee applies to the sale deed. A deed from an executor to an heir is exempt, but the later sale to a buyer is a regular conveyance, so plan for the seller's fee at recording.

What are Camden homes worth, and who owns them?

Camden values sit far below the rest of the Philadelphia area. Census figures for 2020 to 2024 give a median owner-occupied value of $112,000, median gross rent of $1,226, and just 34.4% of the city's 24,443 households as owners. Median household income is $40,546 and 30.2% of residents are in poverty, so many sellers are carrying a house they cannot afford to repair, or an heir inheriting one.

The most common housing type is the rowhouse, much like Philadelphia's. Yorkship Village, now called Fairview, was the nation's first federally funded planned community for working-class residents. The Port of Camden handles wood products, cocoa and other cargo, and the Philadelphia 76ers training complex sits on the waterfront near the Adventure Aquarium, the Battleship New Jersey and the Freedom Mortgage Pavilion.

In October 2025, the state's Economic Development Authority invited proposals for 16 acres on the North Camden waterfront at the former prison site. Camden City School District runs 19 schools and had 7,553 students in 2020-21, with Camden High, Eastside High, Brimm Medical Arts High, Creative Arts Academy and others serving high school grades. It is one of the former Abbott districts for which the state pays school construction costs. Charter and renaissance schools operate alongside the district, which buyers with children will ask about.

Transit is a real selling point. The PATCO Speedline runs 24 hours to Philadelphia and to Collingswood, Haddonfield, Cherry Hill and Lindenwold, and NJ Transit's River Line light rail runs from Camden to Trenton with four stops in the city. The Walter Rand Transportation Center at Martin Luther King Boulevard and Broadway joins PATCO, River Line and NJ Transit buses. By road, Interstate 676 and U.S. 30 lead to the Benjamin Franklin Bridge, Interstate 76 crosses briefly, and Route 168 touches the south. Mean travel time to work is 23.8 minutes.

Camden requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy (the city's building bureau also calls it a Camden Resale Occupancy Certificate) to be applied for and issued before any property in the city is sold or conveyed. If a buyer closes without one, the buyer stays liable for penalties of up to $2,000 until it issues.

The process starts with a zoning permit at City Hall, then an application to the Construction and Building Bureau, followed by four inspections: building, plumbing, electric and fire. All open building permits must be closed first. If the house is not habitable, the buyer can sign an Agreement to Not Occupy and commit to pulling permits and doing the work. Plan submissions are digital only. A change of tenant in a rental is a different step and goes through the Housing Department.

Camden's Bureau of Housing enforces the city's property maintenance code. To schedule an inspection, all taxes must be current, utilities must be on, the fee is paid when scheduling, and the property must be registered with both the Rent Control office and the Municipal Clerk.

The city has had a rent control ordinance since March 12, 1981. At lease expiration a landlord may raise rent by no more than the lower of the 12-month average consumer price index for the Philadelphia area or 6% of the latest rent, and rent cannot rise during a lease. A buyer of a rental building takes on those limits, so a landlord selling should have the registration file ready.

How do taxes and state fees work when selling in Camden?

Camden's Office of Assessments maintains the tax map, processes senior and veteran deductions and exemptions, receives abatement requests, and handles assessment appeals filed with the Camden County Board of Taxation or the New Jersey Tax Court. The office is in City Hall, Room 329, at 520 Market Street. Check that taxes are current before listing, since the city requires current taxes to schedule a rental inspection and a lien can hold up a closing.

New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee falls on the seller. At Camden-level prices below $350,000, the schedule is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 per $500 above that. Senior citizens, blind or disabled sellers and certain low and moderate income housing sales qualify for lower rates, starting at $0.50 per $500 on the first $150,000. The Division of Taxation lists the rates and exemptions.

The seller. The buyer may file as the seller's agent with written permission, but the certificate is issued to the buyer. The application costs $200 plus a separate $64 fire safety fee.

How long is a Camden occupancy certificate application good for?

Six months. After that a new application must be filed and paid for, unless there are open permits on the property.

Can I sell a vacant or damaged house in Camden?

Yes. If the house is not habitable, the buyer can sign an Agreement to Not Occupy and then obtain permits, do the work and apply for the certificate. Open permits have to be closed before a certificate issues.

Yes. Camden has had a rent control ordinance since 1981, with a cap at the lower of the Philadelphia-area consumer price index or 6% at lease expiration, and landlords register each rental unit annually for $25.

Where do I appeal a Camden property assessment?

Appeals go to the Camden County Board of Taxation or the New Jersey Tax Court. The city's Office of Assessments, at 520 Market Street, Room 329, can explain the process and handles deductions.

Where is Carteret and what is the housing like?

Carteret sits in northeastern Middlesex County, on the Arthur Kill across from Staten Island, with the Rahway River forming its northern edge against Linden. Woodbridge Township touches it on every land side. The borough began in 1906 as Roosevelt, carved out of Woodbridge after a referendum, and took the Carteret name in 1922 after an early proprietor of the province. What does the borough require before a Carteret house can close?

Carteret requires a residential certificate of continued occupancy, issued by the Department of Code Enforcement at 61 Cooke Avenue, before a house changes hands. The application asks for the owner, the purchaser, the realtor if there is one, the block and lot, one family or two, the listed price and the names and ages of everyone living there. An addendum to the application works as a plain checklist, and the inspector holds you to it. The seller certifies each item, and the form warns that false statements can be prosecuted with a fine of $2,000 per occurrence.

  • Smoke detectors on each level, plus a smoke detector and carbon monoxide alarm outside every sleeping area, within ten feet.

What happens with Carteret's tax bills at closing?

The borough mails one tax bill a year, in July, with stubs for the installments due on the first day of February, May, August and November. Finance allows ten days of grace after each date. After that, late installments accrue 8 percent a year on up to $1,500 of arrears and 18 percent on any larger amount, counted from the original due date. A delinquency above $10,000 also draws a 6 percent year-end penalty, and balances left open for a year or more are swept into the annual tax sale.

The borough's own advice is to have the latest bill at the closing table, because the buyer's side needs the next installment amount. The tax collector works from the finance department at 100 Cooke Avenue on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. Call (732) 541-3820 extension 3818 for a payoff figure.

If you believe the assessment is off, take it up with the borough assessor first, at extension 3110. Next comes an appeal package from the Middlesex County Tax Board in New Brunswick. The state deadline is April 1, moved to May 1 in a revalued town, and the owner must show the assessed value is unreasonable next to market value. People who hold a senior or veteran deduction also send in an annual statement by March 1 to keep it.

How does Middlesex County record the deed, and which tax forms apply?

Carteret deeds are filed at the Middlesex County Clerk's Registry, 75 Bayard Street, fourth floor, New Brunswick. The office serves the public on weekdays and asks visitors to arrive by 4 p.m. Your attorney or title company usually handles the filing. The county's online search reaches back to 1929 for deeds and 1950 for mortgages, so you can pull your own chain of title before listing, although staff do not run title searches.

Per the county's schedule, a deed costs $45 for page one and $10 for each added page, with a $6 name fee after the fifth name. State charges sit on top of those: the seller owes the realty transfer fee, and every seller hands over a gross income tax form. An out-of-state seller, including a former Carteret resident who has relocated, prepays either two percent of the price or the 8.97 percent rate applied to net gain, unless an exemption listed on the form fits.

Federal rules let an owner keep $250,000 of profit free of tax, or $500,000 for a married couple, after living in the home two of the previous five years, and the state follows that approach.

The quickest routes are a cash purchase from an investor or a short listing of a well-prepared house, and the borough certificate gates both. A cash purchase removes the lender's appraisal and underwriting, yet the inspection, the tax payoff and the deed filing still apply.

A ratio that low indicates assessments sit well below market value, so new values are expected to be higher while the tax rate is meant to fall.

The city's explanation is that a revaluation does not raise the total amount collected. The levy is set by the school, county and municipal budgets, and revaluation spreads it according to value. The presentation's illustration, labeled as an example only, shows a house assessed at $180,000 rising to $540,000 while the rate drops by a factor of three, leaving the bill about the same. The assessor's page lists a $250 deduction for qualifying veterans or surviving spouses and a $250 deduction for seniors or disabled persons. The tax collector's page also links to the state's ANCHOR program for homeowners and renters. If you receive any of these, tell your closing attorney so the adjustments are right.

Where is a Clifton deed recorded and what does the clerk require?

A Clifton deed is recorded with the Passaic County Clerk's Registry Division, 401 Grand Street, Room 113, in Paterson, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. The office does not do title searches, and it does not record surveys. The county lists specific requirements:

  • Deeds must carry the words Prepared by, the tax block, lot and consideration.
  • Every document needs a record and return address, and original signatures with names printed beneath.
  • Use the official county cover sheet, or pay an extra $20 per document.
  • Pay the realty transfer fee with an attorney trust check, title agency trust check, certified check or cash.

The county also posts the seller forms you need: the Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller, the Seller Residency Certification, the Nonresident Seller Tax Declaration and the waiver form. A Clifton owner who has moved out of New Jersey is treated as a nonresident for the sale, which can mean an estimated payment at closing, while a federal principal residence exclusion may shelter up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for a qualifying couple.

No. The city's instructions state that no closing shall take place without a valid Certificate of Inspection, and the certificate expires six months after the fire department inspection.

The standard fee is $125 per unit for a sale. Expedited service costs $200 per unit for a 4 to 20 day turnaround or $300 per unit for four business days.

Inspections run on Wednesdays between 9 a.m. and noon, and an adult over 18 must be home. Call about seven business days afterward, because certificates are picked up in person.

February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a ten-day grace period. Online payment is by e-check only.

The state deadline is April 1, or May 1 in a municipality that has just been revalued. Clifton's revaluation presentation says an appeal must prove value with comparable sales.

English settlers founded Elizabethtown in 1664, and it served as New Jersey's first capital. The state legislature created the City of Elizabeth in 1855 and Union County was formed in 1857. The Singer Sewing Machine plant in Elizabethport once employed thousands, and the company left in 1982.

What is Fair Lawn's history, and how does it show in the housing?

Fair Lawn was farmland before it was a suburb, and the oldest houses on Berdan Avenue and Fair Lawn Avenue still reflect that. Elementary schools are Forrest, Lyncrest, Milnes, Radburn, Warren Point and Westmoreland for kindergarten through fourth grade, and Memorial and Thomas Jefferson middle schools cover grades 5 to 8. Fair Lawn High School had 1,624 students and has been recognized as a Blue Ribbon School.

Employers include Columbia Bank, headquartered in the borough, Kuiken Brothers building materials, Zerega's pasta, and U.S. Technologies. The large Nabisco and Mondelez bakery on Route 208 operated from 1958 and was announced for closure in 2021, with demolition beginning in January 2023. The Fair Lawn Promenade, a mixed-use complex, opened on April 1, 2014. The Broadway shopping district continues to supply local retail jobs.

What are the closing steps and costs in Fair Lawn?

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee when the Bergen County Clerk records the deed, and for a sale over $350,000 the fee runs from $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000 up to $4.80 on the band from $200,000 to $550,000 and $5.30 per $500 between $550,000 and $850,000. Over $1 million, a graduated percent fee also falls on the seller, and your attorney will calculate it.

Sellers who are New Jersey residents, including estates and trusts, complete a GIT/REP-3 to record the deed. For an estate sale, the executors who sign the deed also sign the form, and an executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms. County clerks decide whether to accept a deed, so a rejection should be resolved with the clerk's office first, then with the state GIT/REP Unit at 609-322-9275.

Property tax appeals in Bergen County go to the Board of Taxation at 201-336-6300, and its page says the filing deadline for 2026 assessment appeals has passed. For rent control questions on a rented house, the borough's rent leveling office is at (201) 564-6152.

More questions about Fair Lawn, NJ

Does Fair Lawn require an inspection before I sell?

Yes. The borough requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy for any transfer of title in a one or two family dwelling. The fee is $175, and applications are made in Room 112 of the municipal building. Fire Prevention supplies the smoke certificate at 201-794-5408.

Can a buyer take a Fair Lawn house that fails the inspection?

Yes, with a Conditional Certificate for transfer of title only. The buyer's attorney must send a letter confirming that the buyer understands there is no occupancy, and a failed sidewalk must still be fixed. After closing, the buyer reapplies for the full certificate and pays another $175.

Who signs the GIT/REP form when an estate sells a Fair Lawn house?

The estate completes the form, signed by the executors who sign the deed or by the administrator if there is no will. An executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms, one for the estate and one personally. Residents use the GIT/REP-3.

Why do Fair Lawn addresses have a dash?

The dash comes from the borough's grid numbering system, in use since at least the 1930s. The first number counts blocks from Broadway or follows the numbered street, and addresses south of Broadway start with a zero. Many online forms only accept the number without the dash.

The Bergen County Clerk records deeds, and the Bergen County Board of Taxation handles assessment appeals. The state Realty Transfer Fee and the GIT/REP form go in with the deed. Ask your closing attorney or title company to confirm the filing method for your closing date.

Who is selling a house or unit in Fort Lee, and what do they face?

Fort Lee is a high-rise borough, so a quick sale usually involves the borough's Certificate of Compliance for sales, any association paperwork and, for rented units, rent leveling records. The Census Bureau lists 55.4 percent of homes as owner-occupied, which leaves close to half occupied by renters.

Fort Lee sits on the Hudson Palisades at the eastern edge of Bergen County, at the western end of the George Washington Bridge. The borough covers 2.87 square miles, 12.33 percent of it water, and counted 40,191 people in 2020. The Census estimate for July 2025 is 40,345. The 2020 density was about 15,960 people per square mile of land.

How did Fort Lee get here, and does the history matter to a sale?

Fort Lee began as a Revolutionary War outpost, then became the first center of American filmmaking, and later a skyline of residential towers. Fort Constitution was renamed Fort Lee after General Charles Lee, and in November 1776 Thomas Paine wrote The American Crisis while retreating along what is now Main Street. The New Jersey Legislature formed the borough on March 29, 1904 from remaining parts of Ridgefield Township.

Kalem began filming in Fort Lee in 1907, the Champion Film Company built the first studio in 1909, and many more studios followed during the 1910s and 1920s. The Barrymore Film Center, a theater and film museum that cost $16 million, opened in October 2022.

High-rise apartment construction along Palisade Avenue and Boulevard East began in the 1960s and raised the borough's density sharply. As of 2019 ten structures here, including the bridge, stood over 300 feet. Two 47-story towers called The Modern, finished in 2014 and 2018, are among Bergen County's tallest buildings. For a seller, this means most inventory is built after 1960 and sits under an association or a building management company.

Fort Lee has its own Certificate of Compliance for sales, issued through the Fire Prevention Bureau, and the borough's forms page offers a separate version for rentals. Ask the bureau for the current packet, the inspection fee and the earliest appointment before you fix a closing date.

How do condos, co-ops and associations affect a Fort Lee sale?

Selling a unit in a Fort Lee tower can add association steps before the deed passes. Ask the board or management office what it requires from a seller, whether it issues a resale package, and whether a buyer of a co-op unit needs board approval.

Make that request at the start of the process, before a contract is signed, so the closing date reflects the association's timetable.

For co-op units, the state classifies them as Class 4C property, and the Division of Taxation applies the graduated percent fee to them on deeds above $1 million. The fee starts at 1 percent of the total price for sales between $1,000,000 and $2,000,000 and rises in steps to 3.5 percent above $3.5 million, and the seller is responsible for it.

How do Fort Lee's roads and transit affect buyers?

Fort Lee's position at the George Washington Bridge shapes how buyers judge a property. The bridge, signed as I-95, U.S. 1-9 and U.S. 46, is the world's busiest motor vehicle bridge and carries traffic to Washington Heights in Upper Manhattan.

Roads through the borough include Route 4, Route 5, Route 67, U.S. 9W, U.S. 1/9, U.S. 46, County Route 505, the Palisades Interstate Parkway and Interstate 95. The borough had about 51 miles of roadway in 2010, and the municipality maintained roughly 35 of them.

  • Rockland Coaches runs along Route 9W to Port Authority and the bridge terminal.
  • China Airlines and EVA Air have run private buses from Fort Lee to JFK Airport.

Mean commute time in Fort Lee is 35 minutes, nearly nine minutes above the national mean of 26.4, so buyers will ask how close a building is to a bus stop.

Which schools and neighborhoods define Fort Lee?

The Fort Lee School District serves prekindergarten through twelfth grade with six schools and had 4,074 students in 2021 to 2022. It operates four elementary schools numbered 1 to 4, Lewis F. Cole Middle School for grades 5 to 8, and Fort Lee High School. School 3 won a National Blue Ribbon award in 2010 to 2011. Students can also apply to Bergen County Technical Schools, including the Bergen County Academies in Hackensack.

The borough's named communities include Coytesville, Linwood, Palisade and Taylorville, along with the Palisade Avenue and Boulevard East tower corridor and downtown Main Street. Fort Lee Koreatown, a dining district since the mid-1980s, is a draw for visitors, and Monument Park hosts summer outdoor Shakespeare shows.

Cliffside Park, Edgewater, Englewood, Englewood Cliffs, Leonia, Palisades Park and Ridgefield border the borough. A buyer comparing prices will look at those towns too, so keep your asking price consistent with nearby recent sales.

What are the closing costs and filings for a Fort Lee sale?

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee, which is based on the price recited in the deed. For a sale over $350,000, the rate is $4.80 per $500 for the band from $200,000 to $550,000, which is where a price near Fort Lee's $448,000 median value lands. The deed, the fee and the Gross Income Tax form are filed with the Bergen County Clerk.

Corporations, partnerships and multi-member LLCs file a GIT/REP-3 and check Box 5, and so do single-member LLCs. Individual sellers who live outside New Jersey owe an estimated payment of at least 2 percent of the price, or the gain times 10.75 percent if that is higher, unless the form's assurances apply. The state GIT/REP Unit answers questions at 609-322-9275.

For assessment disputes, the Bergen County Board of Taxation, 201-336-6300, handles appeals, and its page says the 2026 filing deadline has passed.

Does Fort Lee require a certificate to sell a home?

Yes, the borough issues a Certificate of Compliance for sales through its Fire Prevention Bureau. The packet is on the borough's forms page. Ask the bureau for the fee and inspection schedule before setting a closing date.

Are Fort Lee rentals subject to rent leveling?

Fort Lee has a rent leveling office with registration forms for newly rented apartments and for newly rented condo, co-op or one-family units. Landlords should confirm their registrations are current and give the buyer copies. Contact the rent leveling office for the current rules.

What is the mansion tax on a Fort Lee condo sale?

It is the graduated percent fee on deeds above $1 million, and the seller pays it. It starts at 1 percent for sales up to $2 million and reaches 3.5 percent above $3.5 million. It applies to Class 2 residential and Class 4C cooperative units.

How does an LLC sign the seller form in Fort Lee?

An LLC files the GIT/REP-3 and checks Box 5, which covers sellers that are not individuals, estates or trusts. Single-member LLCs follow the same instruction.

The Bergen County Clerk records Fort Lee deeds. The state Realty Transfer Fee and the Gross Income Tax form are filed with the deed. Your closing attorney or title company will handle the submission and confirm the fee.

What are the quickest ways to sell a house in Hoboken, New Jersey?

Hoboken sellers can list on the open market, sell on their own or take a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is. The right one depends on what you own: a condo unit, a rowhouse or a small building with tenants each hit different city offices.

The city's housing stock is dense and mostly renter-occupied, so many sales involve a lease, a registration or a rent ordinance. Sorting those out first shortens the path to a closing date more than any price cut would.

  • Traditional listing: strongest for a renovated unit in good condition, with showings, inspections and a buyer's financing to schedule.
  • Private sale: saves the commission, but you handle disclosures, contracts and the city's resale certificate yourself.
  • Cash purchase: suits a unit with deferred repairs, tenants in place or a deadline, since there is no mortgage approval to wait for.

What is Hoboken's layout and how did the city develop?

Hoboken sits on the west bank of the Hudson River in Hudson County, directly across from Manhattan's West Village and Chelsea. It is called the Mile Square City, though it holds about 1.25 square miles of land and 0.75 square miles of water, for a total of 2 square miles. The ZIP code is 07030.

The street plan is a grid. North-south streets carry names such as Washington, Adams, Jefferson, Madison, Monroe and Jackson, while the numbered east-west streets begin near Observer Highway and end around 16th Street by Weehawken Cove. The Northwest section, once industrial, has been rezoned and rebuilt as housing.

Dutch colonists settled the area in the 17th century, and Hoboken became a township in 1849 and a city in 1855. A steam ferry began running to Manhattan in 1811, and later the rail terminal and shipping lines tied the city to the Port of New York and New Jersey. Maxwell House, Lipton and Hostess once operated here, and the old factory blocks are now condominiums and shops.

What do Census numbers say about Hoboken housing?

Hoboken's 2020 to 2024 estimates show a city of renters with high incomes and high home values. Only about one in three housing units is owner-occupied, so a seller is often competing with a landlord market as well as other owners.

How did Hurricane Sandy change flood questions for Hoboken sellers?

Buyers will ask about flooding, and the history gives them reason. In October 2012 Hurricane Sandy flooded about 1,700 Hoboken homes and caused roughly $100 million in damage, according to the city's encyclopedia entry, and it shut down the PATH station at Hoboken Terminal.

The response was large. The federal housing department set aside $230 million through the Rebuild by Design competition for Hoboken, Weehawken and Jersey City. The city describes a four-part plan: resist surge with barriers, delay runoff with green infrastructure, store rainwater in basins and parks, and discharge it through upgraded sewers and pump stations. Sewer separation work finished in 2022, and the second construction phase began in 2023.

The city's home page also advertises ResilienCity Park, which it calls New Jersey's largest resiliency park, able to hold up to 2 million gallons of rain. When a September 2023 storm dropped 3.5 inches of rain, the entry reports standing water of only a few inches at three of 277 intersections by evening.

If your building took water in 2012, keep repair records, flood insurance history and any elevation paperwork ready. Buyers' attorneys ask for them.

What drives Hoboken's economy and commuting?

Hoboken has the highest share of public transit commuters of any American city, with 56 percent of working residents riding each day. Hoboken Terminal in the southeast corner is a national historic landmark, built in 1907.

  • Rail and subway: NJ Transit's Main, Bergen County, Pascack Valley, Montclair-Boonton, Morris and Essex and Meadowlands lines end at the terminal, and PATH runs to 33rd Street, the World Trade Center and Journal Square.
  • Light rail, bus and ferry: the Hudson-Bergen line has three Hoboken stops, nine NJ Transit bus routes terminate at Hudson Place, and NY Waterway ferries cross to Battery Park City, Pier 11 and West Midtown.
  • Roads: the 14th Street Viaduct leads up to Jersey City Heights, and the Lincoln and Holland tunnels are nearby. The city has no airport.

Major employers include one of the John Wiley and Sons headquarters and, since 2025, a North American headquarters for Unilever at Waterfront Corporate Center. Stevens Institute of Technology supports about 1,285 full-time jobs.

Hoboken Public Schools run five schools with 3,531 students in 2023-24, and three charter schools operate separately.

Which Hoboken city rules apply when you sell or rent out a property?

Three city offices matter most: Construction Code, the Fire Department and Rent Leveling and Stabilization. City Hall is at 94 Washington Street.

Construction Code issues certificates of occupancy for new buildings, additions and altered space, and a certificate of approval for other work. The city's site also carries an application titled Certificate of Smoke Detector, CO and Fire Extinguisher Compliance, which is the form to ask about for a resale. Ask the fire inspection office whether your unit needs it.

Rent Leveling and Stabilization administers Chapter 155, the municipal rent control ordinance. Its staff answer which apartments are covered, what the legal base rent is, and how annual adjustments, vacancy decontrol and surcharges apply. Owners of single-family homes, condominiums, multiple dwellings and mixed-use buildings must register each year through the SDL portal. If you are selling a building with tenants, ask the office for the file on your property and give the buyer's attorney a copy.

How are Hoboken property taxes billed, and what do buyers and sellers owe?

Hoboken sends one tax bill with four quarterly stubs. It combines municipal, school, county and library taxes, plus a Special Improvement District assessment for properties inside that district. The office does not accept postmarks, so a payment counts only when the tax office receives it or it is paid online by the end of the grace period.

Added and omitted assessment bills for improvements go out in October and fall due November 1, with a grace period to November 10. For a lien payoff, call the Tax Collector for a redemption statement, because balances shown on the website may be wrong, and expect to pay by certified check or money order.

Appeals go to the Hudson County Board of Taxation, normally by April 1. A successful judgment is credited first to fourth-quarter taxes, then to any third-quarter balance, and any leftover is refunded to the petitioner or their attorney.

State fees matter at Hoboken prices. With a median owned-home value of $895,100, many sales approach the $1,000,000 line, above which the seller owes a graduated fee of 1 percent of the total price up to $2,000,000 and the buyer owes an extra 1 percent. Residents who keep their New Jersey residency sign GIT/REP-3 at closing instead of making an estimated payment.

More questions about Hoboken, NJ

Is there a rent control law I should know about before selling a Hoboken rental?

Yes. Hoboken enforces Chapter 155, a municipal rent control ordinance, through its Rent Leveling and Stabilization office. The office can tell you which apartments are covered, the legal base rent and the allowed increases. Owners register their properties every year through the SDL portal, and the office keeps a public file on each residential property.

Does Hoboken require a certificate to sell a home?

The city publishes an application for a Certificate of Smoke Detector, CO and Fire Extinguisher Compliance, and Construction Code issues certificates of occupancy for new or altered space. Ask the fire inspection office and your closing attorney which one your sale needs, since it can differ for a condo, a rowhouse and a multi-unit building.

Does Hoboken flood, and what should a seller have ready?

Parts of the city flooded badly in Hurricane Sandy in 2012, and the city has since built sewer, park and barrier projects with $230 million in federal funds. Buyers and their attorneys ask about past water damage, so gather repair records and insurance history for your address and review them with your attorney before listing.

When are Hoboken property taxes due?

In four quarterly installments listed on the single annual bill. The Tax Collector charges interest back to the due date once the grace period ends, and does not honor postmarks. Pay online or deliver the check to City Hall at 94 Washington Street, and call the office for a redemption figure if a lien exists.

How long do I have to appeal my Hoboken assessment?

Generally until April 1, filed with the Hudson County Board of Taxation on Form A-1. Owners of properties assessed above $1,000,000 may go straight to the Tax Court by the same date. If you disagree with the board's judgment, the Tax Court appeal must be filed within 45 days.

What should I know about selling a house in Egg Harbor Township, NJ?

Egg Harbor Township is a large Atlantic County municipality, 75.47 square miles of which 67.05 is land, and it is separate from Egg Harbor City, which has its own entry in the state's municipality lists. The Census Bureau estimates 48,435 residents for 2025. Owner-occupancy is high at 84.4 percent, the median owner-occupied home value is $312,700, and median household income is $97,190.

Both the home value and the owner share lead to one practical point for sellers: most houses here are owned, not rented, and the main pre-closing task is the state fire-safety certificate.

Does Egg Harbor Township require a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate?

New Jersey's Division of Fire Safety runs an online smoke certification application with "Change of Ownership" as a stated reason, and it asks for the closing date, block, lot and whether you are the seller or the buyer's representative. Sheriff's sales, foreclosures, forfeitures and purchases from a federal agency work differently: the new owner must obtain the certificate before moving in. A building that is uninhabitable and will be rehabilitated or demolished can be exempt from the certificate, but it cannot be occupied until a new certificate of occupancy comes from the local construction official.

For the township's own form, fee and timing, ask the Bureau of Fire Inspections before you set a closing date.

How settled is the Egg Harbor Township housing market?

Census data show a population up 1.2 percent from the April 2020 base of 47,849 to 48,435 in 2025. The township has 17,261 households averaging 2.78 people, and 93.6 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier.

  • Median owner costs are $2,371 a month with a mortgage and $954 without one.
  • Median gross rent is $1,456.
  • 17.7 percent of residents were born abroad, and 29.8 percent speak another language at home.
  • Veterans number 2,166.

The township's density is 713.6 people per square mile, a fraction of the Elizabeth or Englewood figure.

How did the township get its shape?

Lenape families summered near Bargaintown Lake and along Patcong Creek. A 1694 act placed the Egg Harbour settlers under Gloucester County, and Atlantic County was separated in 1837. Since then, ten municipalities have split from the original township, among them Atlantic City in 1854, Somers Point in 1886 and Ventnor City in 1903.

What remains is spread out. The seat of government is in Bargaintown, and the township includes Cardiff, English Creek, Farmington, Scullville, Steelmanville and West Atlantic City, plus part of McKee City. West Atlantic City and Anchorage Poynte are not contiguous with the main body. A listing should name the section, because buyers search by those names.

How do the Pinelands rules affect a house here?

The township is one of 56 South Jersey municipalities in the Pinelands National Reserve, and part of it lies in the state-designated Pinelands Area. The Pinelands Commission classed Egg Harbor Township, Hamilton and Galloway as Regional Growth Areas, which pushed residential building here so that trees in the preserved Pine Barrens stay standing.

  • In 2007 the planning board approved 667 homes in the Farmington section: townhouses, homes for buyers 55 and older, and single-family houses.
  • If your lot sits near wetlands or protected land, ask the township's construction office about limits before planning a deck, shed or addition.
  • Wildlife management areas including Malibu Beach, Pork Island and Lester G. MacNamara are public land in the south and east.

What does the township offer commuters and families?

The Atlantic City Expressway crosses the township for 5.3 miles and meets the Garden State Parkway at Interchange 7, which is Parkway Interchange 38. The Parkway runs 8.6 miles through, and Routes 40, 322 and 9 plus county routes 559, 563, 575 and 585 carry local traffic. NJ Transit buses 502, 507, 508 and 509 link the township with Atlantic City. Most of Atlantic City International Airport lies in the northern part of the township. The Census puts mean travel to work at 23.3 minutes, the shortest of the four towns.

The township has 297 miles of roads, 207 of them municipal. Harbor Square, the former Shore Mall, is the regional shopping center, and the Atlantic County Bikeway runs 7.5 miles from the mall toward Hamilton Township.

What draws buyers to the township besides the price?

  • Malibu Beach Wildlife Management Area covers 95.7 acres of marsh, dunes and back-bay shoreline and is known locally as Dog Beach, one of the few New Jersey beaches that permits dogs.
  • Storybook Land, a 20 acre children's park, opened in 1955 on the township's mainland side.
  • The township was one of the first five in the state, in 2017, to authorize medical cannabis dispensaries.
  • The township borders Ocean City and has Great Egg Harbor Bay shoreline in its eastern segment.

Name the nearest of these in your listing, since they are what a buyer from outside Atlantic County will recognize.

Which schools serve Egg Harbor Township homes?

Egg Harbor Township Schools run seven schools for pre-kindergarten through grade 12. The 2023-24 enrollment was 7,473 students with a 10.9 to 1 student-teacher ratio. Davenport and Swift-Slaybaugh serve the early grades, the Dr. Joyanne D. Miller school takes grades 4 and 5, Alder Avenue and Fernwood Avenue are the middle schools, and Egg Harbor Township High School had 2,299 students. Students can also go to the Atlantic County Institute of Technology in Mays Landing or the Charter-Tech High School for the Performing Arts in Somers Point.

How do I appeal an assessment or record a deed in Atlantic County?

Atlantic County's Board of Taxation sits in Mays Landing at 5909 Main Street and can be reached at (609) 645-5820. Petitions are due by April 1, and hearings are typically held between April and September at the Historic Courthouse. The board mails a hearing notice at least ten days ahead, and any comparable sales you rely on must reach the board, the municipal assessor and the municipal clerk at least seven days before the hearing. Good comparables are real sales in the same town within the year before the prior October 1; most foreclosures, sheriff's sales, estate sales and short sales are treated as not usable. A reduction comes back as a credit through a revised bill from the tax collector, and you have 45 days from the judgment to go to the State Tax Court.

No. The state lists Egg Harbor Township and Egg Harbor City as separate municipalities. This page covers the township, which had 48,435 residents in the 2025 Census estimate.

Yes, a change of ownership calls for a state smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. Ask the township's Bureau of Fire Inspections for its form, fee and timing before you pick a closing date.

The Census Bureau reports $312,700 for owner-occupied homes in the 2020 to 2024 period, and 84.4 percent of homes are owner occupied.

When is the Atlantic County tax appeal deadline?

April 1 of the tax year, filed with the Atlantic County Board of Taxation. Where a revaluation was done, the deadline is May 1.

How long are Atlantic County hearing notices sent in advance?

At least ten days before the hearing. Comparable sales evidence is due to the board, the assessor and the clerk at least seven days before.

What should an Evesham Township owner know before selling quickly?

Evesham Township is a large South Jersey suburb in Burlington County, and a quick sale there depends mostly on a short list of local steps: a resale certificate through the fire department, permits for past work, and the state paperwork filed with the deed.

The township covers about 29 square miles and counted 46,826 people in 2020. The Census Bureau estimated 49,525 residents in July 2025, which makes Evesham the most populous municipality in Burlington County. People often say Marlton when they mean Evesham, because Marlton is the best known community inside the township and shares ZIP code 08053 with much of it.

Part of the township sits inside the Pinelands Area, a state-designated zone with its own land use rules. If your lot is near the wooded edge of town, check the zoning map before you describe the property to a buyer, since it affects what a purchaser can add or build later.

How old is Evesham, and why does the history matter to a seller?

Evesham dates to the late 1600s, so many parcels carry old deeds and older houses sit beside postwar subdivisions. Quakers settled the area in 1672, and the township was established in 1688 as Eversham in the Province of West Jersey. It was incorporated again under the 1798 Township Act on February 21, 1798.

The original township was far larger. The population climbed from 4,548 in 1960 to 35,309 in 1990, so a large share of the housing stock went up in a single generation.

Title searches on older parcels can turn up easements or old liens that a closing attorney has to clear before the deed records.

What do Census figures say about Evesham homes and owners?

Evesham is an owner-occupied township with prices above the national median, according to Census QuickFacts. The table below sets the township against the country using the 2020 to 2024 estimates.

Which roads and transit lines affect an Evesham sale?

Route 70 and Route 73 are the two highways that define the township, and buyers judge a house by how it connects to them. Route 70 crosses the northern part of Evesham from east to west, Route 73 runs along the western border, and County Route 544 (Marlton Parkway and Taunton Lake Road) links the two.

The old Marlton Circle at Routes 70 and 73 once handled about 90,000 vehicles a day and was the site of as many as 175 crashes a year. A grade-separated interchange replaced it in 2011, and the change made commutes toward Philadelphia and Cherry Hill more predictable.

  • NJ Transit bus route 406 runs through the township between Berlin and Philadelphia.
  • The Atco station, just across the border in Waterford Township, carries Atlantic City Line trains to Philadelphia 30th Street and the Atlantic City Rail Terminal.
  • The township reported about 183 miles of roadway in 2010, with the municipality maintaining about 159 of them.

Which schools serve Evesham homes?

Evesham Township School District covers prekindergarten through eighth grade, and Cherokee High School takes students from ninth through twelfth grade. In the 2021 to 2022 school year the local district ran eight schools and enrolled 4,384 students.

The elementary schools named in the district are Beeler, DeMasi, Jaggard, Marlton, Rice and Van Zant, and the two middle schools are DeMasi and Marlton Middle. Cherokee High School had 2,165 students that year after a 210,000 square foot addition opened in 2001.

Families searching for a house usually sort by elementary school zone, so name the school attached to your address in the listing or in any direct conversation with a buyer.

What does Evesham require before a house changes hands?

Evesham directs residential resale certificate requests to the Evesham Township Fire Department, and the fire department's own site, eveshamfire.org, is where inspection scheduling and fees are posted. Start that request early so the certificate is ready when the closing date arrives.

The Community Development office handles permits from the Township Building at 984 Tuckerton Road in Marlton, Room 204, Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The construction office can be reached at 856-983-2914, then option 4. Its published guidance is direct about unpermitted work: a construction permit confirms that work meets fire and building codes, and an insurer can refuse a claim tied to work done without one.

  • Sheds and fences need a zoning permit, and a fence around a pool also needs a building permit meeting the pool barrier code.
  • A homeowners association may need to approve a shed or fence first.
  • Interior sump pump or French drain work needs a construction permit, while exterior-only drainage work does not.
  • Flood zone questions can be checked on the FEMA Flood Map Service Center and the township mapping portal.

If a past owner finished a basement, deck or pool without paperwork, sort that out before you list. A buyer's attorney will ask for permit history, and a gap can stall a sale for weeks.

Can you sell an Evesham rental or short-term rental house?

Yes, but the rental registration and fire inspection records go with the property, so gather them first. Evesham treats short-term rentals such as Airbnb and Vrbo listings like long-term rentals: they must pass a fire department inspection and register with the Township Clerk's Office.

The township requires a Certificate of Smoke Alarm, Carbon Monoxide Alarm, and Portable Fire Extinguisher Compliance each time a new tenant occupies the property, under N.J.A.C. 5:70-2.3. Failing to comply carries a $500 penalty, and the fire department sets the fees for the inspection.

If tenants live in the house, a buyer will want the lease, the deposit amount and the last inspection certificate. A cash purchaser who wants the house empty should say so in writing before the contract is signed, so that notice periods can be planned. For landlord and tenant disputes, the township points residents to the Burlington County court system and Legal Services of New Jersey.

What does the seller handle at closing in Evesham?

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee and signs a Gross Income Tax residency form, and both are filed with the deed at the Burlington County Clerk. The Division of Taxation charges the fee per $500 of the price recited in the deed. For a standard sale over $350,000, the band from $200,000 to $550,000 is $4.80 per $500, which is the band a price near Evesham's median home value reaches.

Homes sold above $1 million add a graduated percent fee that the seller owes, starting at 1 percent of the total price. Most Evesham sales fall well under that line.

The Gross Income Tax form for most New Jersey residents is the GIT/REP-3. Burlington County notified filers that any GIT/REP form signed on or after October 1, 2025 must be the current version, and older versions are rejected at recording. Questions go to the state GIT/REP Unit at 609-322-9275. Nonresident sellers owe an estimated payment of at least 2 percent of the price unless an exemption applies.

The Burlington County Clerk also runs a free Property Fraud Alert system that alerts owners when a document is recorded in their name, and it is worth joining before and after a sale.

How does a fast as-is sale in Evesham usually move?

A fast sale follows a short sequence, and each step has a clear owner. The steps below assume you have clear title and no open permits.

  • Gather the deed, the last tax bill, any rental registration and your mortgage payoff figure.
  • Request the fire department resale certificate and fix anything it flags, or agree in the contract who fixes it.
  • Have your closing attorney order the title search and prepare the deed with the RTF and GIT/REP filings.
  • Close, hand over keys, and let the attorney record the deed with the Burlington County Clerk.

Cash buyers often agree to take a house in its current condition, which removes repair negotiations but not the certificate or the state filings. Ask any buyer to put the price, the closing date and who pays for each inspection in one written document before you commit.

Do I need a certificate from the township to sell my house in Evesham?

Yes, residential resales go through the Evesham Township Fire Department for a certificate. The township construction pages send resale and rental requests there, and eveshamfire.org lists scheduling and fees. Ask for the inspection date as soon as you decide to sell.

What happens if work on my Evesham house was done without a permit?

A buyer's attorney will likely require it to be resolved before closing. The township says a construction permit confirms work meets fire and building codes, and an insurer may deny a claim tied to unpermitted work. Call the construction office at 856-983-2914, option 4, to learn what a retroactive permit needs.

Who pays the realty transfer fee in an Evesham sale?

The seller pays it. The state charges it when the deed is recorded with the Burlington County Clerk, based on the price in the deed, and an extra graduated fee applies above $1 million. Your closing attorney or title company will calculate the exact figure.

Can I sell a house in Evesham if I live out of state?

Yes. A nonresident seller files a GIT/REP form and pays an estimated Gross Income Tax of at least 2 percent of the price at closing unless an exemption on the form applies. The payment can be claimed back against the final tax owed when you file.

Is part of Evesham in the Pinelands?

Yes, a portion of the township lies in the state-designated Pinelands Area, and the township zoning map and Pinelands Commission maps show which lots are covered. Check your parcel before marketing the property, since Pinelands rules may affect additions or new structures.

What sets a Cherry Hill home sale apart from a typical New Jersey closing?

Cherry Hill sellers face two separate township inspections before closing, one covering the property's exterior and one covering smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, and each is booked through a different office. Booking both early keeps the closing date from slipping.

The township is large, mostly owner-occupied and built largely in the decades after World War II, so the typical seller owns a single-family house on a suburban lot with trees, fences, driveways and sidewalks that the township cares about. This page walks through the inspections, the tax calendar, the county recording charges and a worked transfer-fee example so you can set a realistic closing date.

How big is Cherry Hill and how did it develop?

Cherry Hill covers about 24 square miles of Camden County, which makes it the county's most populous municipality. It began as Delaware Township in 1844, and in 1961 took the Cherry Hill name from a local farm. Quaker settlers arrived in the late 1600s, the first small cluster was Colestown, and 19th-century farms supplied produce to the Campbell's soup plant across the river in Camden. Growth then jumped after World War II, from about 10,400 residents in 1950 to 31,500 in 1960 and 64,400 in 1970.

Its neighborhoods include Ashland, Barclay, Erlton, Greentree, Kingston Estates, Springdale, Woodcrest and the area around Cherry Hill Mall. Pennsauken Creek marks the eastern line with Burlington County, the Cooper River runs along the southern border beside Route 70, and Haddonfield, Collingswood and Voorhees sit across those lines.
