With three of every four homes owner-occupied and a middle value near $386,000, the typical listing is a family house where condition, curb appeal and school zone matter more than rental income.

Which roads, transit lines and schools matter to Cherry Hill buyers?

Cherry Hill is built around highway access to Philadelphia. Interstate 295 has three exits in the township, including exit 31, which leads directly to the Woodcrest PATCO station, and Routes 38, 41, 70 and 154 cross it. Township roads total about 309 miles, of which the township itself maintains roughly 247. NJ Transit buses reach Philadelphia on the 317, 404 and 406 routes, and the Atlantic City Line stops at the Cherry Hill station.

Schools are the other big talking point. Cherry Hill Public Schools operates 19 schools with about 10,800 students in the 2023 to 2024 school year, including two traditional high schools, Cherry Hill High School East and Cherry Hill High School West, three middle schools and 12 elementary schools. Private options include Camden Catholic High School and the King's Christian School.

  • Mention the PATCO station and I-295 exits in your listing if you are close to them.
  • Name the elementary school zone, since buyers search by it.
  • Note any Cooper River or creek frontage and have the drainage history ready.

What are the two Cherry Hill inspections before closing?

A seller here needs a Certificate of Continued Occupancy from the township and a smoke alarm and carbon monoxide compliance certificate from the fire department. A single-family sale cannot reach closing without them, and they are separate appointments with separate costs.

The occupancy certificate comes from Community Development, which handles property maintenance, at 820 Mercer Street, Room 202. The property maintenance officer looks at exterior areas only. The township lists these items:

  • Sidewalks, driveways and fences.
  • Trees and natural growth.
  • Sanitation and exhaust vents.
  • Grading and drainage, including where sump pumps discharge.
  • Accessory structures and ground surface hazards.

The inspection costs $100, payable ahead of the visit, and you can apply online, in person or by mail. Online applications need office approval before a payment request is emailed, cancellations after payment are not refunded, and the property maintenance line is 856-834-3364. Some condominiums and townhomes are excluded, and the township posts a list of properties that skip the inspection.

The fire department certificate is a different step. It is required for one- and two-family homes before settlement, and sellers are asked to request the appointment three to four weeks early. If the home passes and payment is made, the certificate is handed over at the visit; temporary certificates are not issued, and fire extinguishers are no longer required. The fire department's inspection line is (856) 429-7441. Because the two appointments run on separate calendars, book both the week the contract is signed.

Does the township help with move-out trash after a Cherry Hill sale?

Yes, Cherry Hill offers a one-time courtesy collection for house clean-outs after a sale, covering furniture, carpets, bedding and similar household items. Proof that you applied for a Continued Certificate of Occupancy is required before Public Works will schedule it, pickups happen on Fridays, and the number to call is 856-424-4422.

The same guidelines say no trash or recycling service goes to dwellings under construction, vacant lots or properties lacking a valid certificate of occupancy, so a vacant house waiting on its paperwork may go without pickup. Plan the clean-out around the certificate date, and keep contractor debris out of the cart, because construction waste generated by a contractor has to be hauled away by that contractor.

When are Cherry Hill property taxes due and who collects them?

The four installments land on the first of August, November, February and May, and a ten-day grace period rolls forward to the next business day if it ends on a weekend or holiday. The township mails two bills a year: July covers the third and fourth installments, and January covers the first and second. Money has to be in the tax office by the last grace day, because postmarks do not count.

Late payments accrue 8 percent a year up to $1,500 of arrears and 18 percent on any amount beyond that, running from the original due date. The tax collector also bills sewer rent: residential sewer is a flat annual fee due April 1, with a 10 percent discount for owners 60 or older who live in the property. Ask the tax office at 856-488-7880 for a closing figure that includes any sewer balance. The office gathers money for the school district, the fire district and Camden County along with the township, so the bill you pay includes those shares.

Appeals follow state deadlines, April 1 or May 1 after a revaluation, and go to the Camden County Board of Taxation.

How much is the transfer fee and where does the deed get filed?

The Camden County Clerk files the deed, and the seller owes the state realty transfer fee when it is filed. Above $350,000 the state schedule runs $2.90 per $500 for the first $150,000, $4.25 per $500 for the slice from $150,000 to $200,000 and $4.80 per $500 for the slice from $200,000 to $550,000. On a $400,000 price, those slices add up to about $3,215: $870, then $425, then $1,920. Confirm the figure with your closing attorney, since senior, disabled and low-income rates run lower.

The county's recording schedule lists $30 for page one of a deed, $10 for every added page, a $10 abstracting fee and a $5 homeless trust fund charge, with a $55 floor. Camden County's online land records start in 1978, and the clerk's office answers at 856-225-5300. A New Jersey resident signs a residency certification at closing, while a seller who is leaving the state prepays estimated income tax, so tell your attorney early if you are relocating.

Yes, two of them. The township requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy for single-family resale, and the fire department requires a smoke alarm and carbon monoxide compliance certificate before settlement.

What does the Cherry Hill resale inspection cost?

The occupancy inspection is $100, paid before the inspector arrives. The fire department sets its own charges, which are posted on its checklist.

How early should the Cherry Hill fire inspection be scheduled?

Three to four weeks before settlement. The certificate is given at the appointment if the home complies and payment is made, and temporary certificates are not available.

What are the Cherry Hill tax installment dates?

August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. A ten-day grace period applies, and the money must reach the tax office by then because postmarks do not count.

The Camden County Clerk. The posted schedule lists $30 for page one of a deed, $10 for each added page, a $10 abstracting fee and a $5 homeless trust fund charge.

What is Belleville's history and where does it sit in Essex County?

Belleville grew from a settlement called Second River, renamed Belleville in 1797, and it was incorporated as a township in 1839 from part of Bloomfield. The township reincorporated as a town in 1910 and voted to become a township again in 1981. Congress passed a resolution in 1994 recognizing Belleville as the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution in the United States.

The township borders Bloomfield, Newark and Nutley in Essex County, Lyndhurst and North Arlington in Bergen County, and Kearny in Hudson County. The Second River forms much of the border with Newark through Branch Brook Park, and Belleville calls itself the Cherry Blossom Capital of America because of the park's spring display. Silver Lake, split between Belleville and Bloomfield, is the best-known unincorporated community, alongside Belwood, Big Tree and Soho.

The local economy is also worth a line in a listing. Belleville Township spans only 3.37 square miles in total, so most blocks are within a short walk of a bus line or a commercial street.

Which roads, transit and schools help Belleville sell?

Route 7, Route 21 and County Route 506 pass through Belleville, and the Belleville Turnpike Bridge, also called the Rutgers Street Bridge, crosses the Passaic River to North Arlington. The Silver Lake station provides Newark Light Rail service to Newark Penn Station, and NJ Transit buses 13, 27, 72, 74, 90, 92, 93 and 94 run to Newark. The census puts average commute time at 32.4 minutes.

The Belleville School District has 10 schools and 5,095 students in 2023-24, according to Wikipedia's summary of federal data. The township's own links also point residents to Clara Maass Medical Center, and census figures show health care and social assistance receipts of about $807 million in 2022, the largest business total reported for the township.

  • Vacant / Abandoned Property Registration, which applies if the house is empty.
  • Request for List of Owners within 200 Feet, used for planning board and zoning board applications.
  • Zoning Permit Application, Fence Permit Application and Pool Permits, which show what work was approved.
  • Landlord Identity Registration Form, filed with the Township Clerk.
  • Fire Department items such as the Fire Safety Permit, a Home Fire Protection Plan and a Fire Safety Checklist for Homeowners and Renters.

Gather the permit paperwork for any work you finished in the house, including fences, pools and driveways, since the township keeps separate applications for each. Having those approvals ready lets a buyer's attorney confirm the work was permitted without waiting on township offices.

How do rent leveling and landlord rules affect a Belleville sale?

Belleville has a Rent Leveling Board, and its forms include a Vacancy Decontrol Application and a Rent Leveling Complaint Form. If you own a rental, check with the board about registration, any open complaints and whether a vacancy decontrol filing is on file before a buyer's attorney asks.

Buyers of tenant-occupied buildings will want copies of leases and the rent roster, so organize them before you list. A clean file shortens attorney review and reduces last-minute price talks.

What property tax and relief records should I gather in Belleville?

Belleville's Tax Assessor page carries a Property Assessment form and a Guide to Appeal Hearings, and the Tax Collector page carries the PD-5 Senior Property Tax Deduction form, a Veteran's Property Tax Credit form and an online payment portal. The township also links the Essex County Board of Taxation and the state's Property Tax Relief Program.

Pull your latest tax bill and any open balance before you list, because buyers and title companies ask for them. If you have a PD-5 deduction or veteran's credit, the buyer will not inherit it automatically, so ask the Tax Collector whether those benefits change after a sale. The township website also lists a Home Improvement Program with an application and a contractor application, which a buyer planning repairs can read.

How can you sell a house fast in Irvington, New Jersey?

An Irvington owner can hire an agent, sell without one or take a cash offer for the house in its current state. Whichever it is, the township wants a housing inspection before title passes. That requirement drives the timeline, so begin it when you decide to sell.

Fewer than one in three housing units here is owner-occupied, so a good number of sellers are landlords or heirs. The inspection fee scales with the number of dwelling units in the building.

  • Listing: best for a house that will pass inspection with little work and appraise well.
  • Private sale: works if you can manage the inspection, the contract and the buyer's financing without an agent.
  • Cash sale: fits a house with code violations, tenants or probate complications, because the purchase contract can be written around the condition.

Where is Irvington and how did it get its name?

Irvington is a small, dense township of 2.92 square miles in Essex County. Maplewood lies to the west and Newark to the east, with Hillside and Union to the south and southwest. The Elizabeth River runs through it near Civic Square.

Until the middle of the 1800s the place was called Camptown. After a well-known ballad about Camptown races was published in 1850, residents worried about the association and renamed it for the author Washington Irving. It became an incorporated village on March 27, 1874, a town in 1898, and a township after a 1982 referendum.

An amusement park, Olympic Park, straddled the Irvington and Maplewood line from 1887 to 1965. Population rose from 1,677 in 1880 to 56,733 in 1930. It has stayed between about 54,000 and 61,500 since then, reaching 61,176 in the 2020 census and an estimated 62,233 in July 2025.

What do Census figures show about Irvington housing and residents?

Irvington is a rental-heavy township with the lowest home values of the four municipalities in the same Census comparison. QuickFacts shows owners in 29.6 percent of units, with a median owned home worth $335,600.

Rent at the median is $1,386 a month. Owners pay $2,489 with a mortgage and $1,026 without. Across 23,542 households of roughly 2.57 people, median income is $61,609, and 19.0 percent of residents fall below the poverty line.

Foreign-born residents account for 35.5 percent of the population, and 32.4 percent of people aged 5 and up speak another language at home. If several relatives share ownership, a short written summary of key dates in their own language keeps everyone on schedule.

What does the Certificate of Housing Compliance require when you sell in Irvington?

Irvington's code makes it unlawful to sell, convey or transfer a building with residential units, or for a buyer to take title or possession, until a Certificate of Housing Compliance has been issued. The Department of Housing issues it after an application and an inspection. The online portal at irvingtonportal.us handles the application and the separate Fire Department inspection.

For an as-is sale, the contract must be attached to the application and signed by both seller and buyer. If the inspection finds violations that stay unrepaired, the director may issue the temporary certificate, and the buyer then acknowledges the duty to fix them. Liability for skipping the certificate falls on both the owner and the purchaser.

The code's exemption section lists transfers between immediate family members, a property inspected within the prior six months, a purchase made to demolish the building and probate transfers to heirs under a will. Ask the Housing Department how those exemptions apply to your sale. A denied certificate can be appealed in writing to the Business Administrator, who must decide within five business days.

Where do you apply, and who inspects?

The Housing and Building office sits in the Municipal Building, Room 201, at 1 Civic Square. Its page lists an evening housing inspector available Monday to Friday from 5:00 to 9:00 p.m. and Saturday from 9:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m., which helps working owners schedule around a job.

  • Owners of any building in the township, residential or commercial, must give the Housing Department, Tax Collector and Tax Assessor their true home address and company address.
  • Vacant properties go through the Vacant Property Registration Program, with registration on the township portal.
  • Violation notices become orders if no written petition for a hearing is filed within 10 days, so respond to any notice quickly.
  • Fines under the property maintenance code run from $50 for a first violation to $1,000 for a fourth, which also requires a court appearance.

Of the 69.44 miles of road within the township, Irvington maintains 55.98.

How do roads, buses and schools shape the Irvington housing market?

Irvington sits between Newark and the suburbs, and transit is a selling point. The Garden State Parkway passes through the center of the township with exits 143 and 144. Interstate 78 touches the southeastern edge at Exit 54, and County Road 509 is the main local road.

  • Buses: the Irvington Bus Terminal on Springfield Avenue is one of NJ Transit's busiest. Route 107 reaches the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Midtown, and nine routes run to Newark.
  • Air: Newark Liberty International Airport is in neighboring Newark and Elizabeth.
  • Schools: Irvington Public Schools run pre-kindergarten through grade 12 and are one of 31 former Abbott districts. The district had 12 schools and 8,020 students in 2019-20.
  • Business incentives: parts of the township lie in an Urban Enterprise Zone established in May 1996, which expires in May 2027 and allows a reduced 3.3125 percent sales tax at eligible merchants. The area around the bus terminal became a state-designated transit village in July 2015.

What do taxes, recording and state fees add to an Irvington sale?

Deeds for all 22 Essex County municipalities are recorded by the county Register of Deeds and Mortgages, whose files reach back to 1637. Assessment appeals are filed with the Essex County Board of Taxation on Form A-1, normally by April 1, and the Tax Court hears further appeals filed within 45 days of the board's judgment.

State law puts the Realty Transfer Fee on the seller. Because Irvington's median owned home, $335,600, sits under $350,000, the lower schedule governs, topping out at $3.90 per $500 for the slice between $200,000 and $350,000. A landlord living outside New Jersey files GIT/REP-1 and prepays tax of 2 percent of the price or 8.97 percent of the net gain, unless the form's exemptions apply.

Do I need a certificate to sell my house in Irvington?

Yes. The Township Code requires a Certificate of Housing Compliance before any building with residential units is sold, conveyed or transferred. The Housing Department issues it after an application and an inspection, and a Fire Department inspection is also required, with both started on the township's online portal.

How much does the Irvington sale inspection cost?

The code sets $237 per dwelling unit up to three units in a building and $116 for each unit above three. A single-family house therefore costs $237 and a three-family $711. Reinspections carry their own fee, so fix the listed items before the first visit and confirm current amounts with the Housing Department.

Can I sell an Irvington house as-is if it has violations?

Yes, with conditions. The as-is contract must be attached to the application and signed by both parties. If violations remain unrepaired at closing, the director may issue a nonrenewable temporary certificate lasting up to six months, and the buyer acknowledges in writing the duty to bring the property into compliance.

The code's exemption section lists family transfers, a property inspected within six months before the transfer, a purchase for demolition and probate transfers to heirs under a will. The wording is older than the latest amendments, so ask the Housing Department to confirm in writing that an exemption covers your sale.

Where is the deed recorded for an Irvington sale?

At the Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages, which covers the county's 22 municipalities. A title company or attorney typically files the deed together with the transfer fee affidavit and GIT/REP form, so you seldom visit in person.

How did Ewing Township grow into the community it is today?

Ewing became a township on February 22, 1834, cut from Trenton Township and named in honor of Charles Ewing, a former chief justice of the New Jersey Supreme Court. It joined the new Mercer County in 1838. Before that the land was mostly farms and small hamlets: Carleton is now Ewing, Cross Keys is Ewingville, and Birmingham is West Trenton.

The township grew as a suburb of Trenton through the 20th century. Its population rose from 6,942 in 1930 to 26,628 by 1960 and has stayed between about 32,800 and 37,300 since 1970. Blocks near the Trenton line are distinctly urban, while most of the township is residential subdivisions.

Neighborhood names show up in listings and appraisals, so use the local one. Examples include Ewingville, West Trenton, Prospect Heights, Fernwood, Hillwood Lakes, Parkway Village, Scudders Falls and Wilburtha. Many were built in separate phases, and house styles change noticeably from one to the next.

Ewing prices sit below the national median value, and rental households make up a third of the township. The table lists the 2020 to 2024 Census QuickFacts estimates against national figures.

Which employers and institutions anchor the Ewing market?

Ewing hosts several large public employers, which keeps demand for housing steady among staff who want a short commute. The Katzenbach School for the Deaf and the Trenton-Mercer Airport are also located in the township.

Church and Dwight moved its corporate headquarters from Princeton to Ewing in 2013. The township also absorbed a major loss: the Naval Air Warfare Center Trenton on Parkway Avenue operated from 1953 until 1997 and closed under the 1993 base closure recommendations, ending nearly 700 civilian positions. The Jones Farm, the last working farm in Ewing, shut at the end of 2022.

  • Education and public safety: The College of New Jersey and State Police headquarters.
  • State agencies: the Department of Transportation headquarters and Trenton Psychiatric Hospital.
  • Private employers: Church and Dwight, plus the Community Blood Council of New Jersey.

Which roads and rail lines serve Ewing homes?

Four major roads cross the township, and the West Trenton rail terminal anchors the commuter side. Interstate 295 crosses the northwest corner, Route 29 follows the Delaware River as the Delaware River Scenic Byway, U.S. Route 206 skirts the southeast, and Route 31 (Pennington Road) runs north to Pennington and Flemington.

West Trenton station is the terminus of SEPTA's West Trenton Line, which mainly carries riders to Philadelphia. NJ Transit buses 601, 607, 608, 609 and 624 connect the township with Trenton. Trenton-Mercer Airport, open since 1929 and served by Frontier Airlines, is also inside Ewing's borders.

The Delaware and Raritan Canal passes near the river, and the strip of land along it is part of the Delaware and Raritan Canal State Park. Homes along River Road and Route 29 sit near the water, so check flood-zone status with the township before quoting a price to a buyer who asks.

How do schools and weather affect an Ewing house?

Ewing Public Schools run prekindergarten through twelfth grade in one district, with five schools: Antheil, Lore and Parkway elementary schools, Fisher Middle School and Ewing High School. Enrollment was 3,444 students in the 2020 to 2021 school year. The district is also known for the 1946 case Everson v. Board of Education, a U.S. Supreme Court decision on bus transport for parochial school students.

The climate is hot-summer humid continental. Based on 1991 to 2020 normals, the township averages 48.2 inches of precipitation a year and about 8 inches of snow in each of January and February.

That much rain is why the housing inspector looks at grading and drainage, roofs, gutters and foundation walls. Fixing a downspout that empties against the foundation costs little and removes an easy objection before the inspection.

What does Ewing's resale inspection check?

Every dwelling or commercial building offered for resale must be inspected and approved by the Ewing Division of Housing, and the residential fee on the township's 2025 form is $125. The inspector works from the International Property Maintenance Code and township ordinances. Requests can be made through the township's SDL portal, which needs an account, or through the Construction Office at 1666 Pennington Road, 609-883-2900, extension 7676.

The township's printed checklist is not limited to these items, but they come up often:

  • Smoke alarms on every level, using ten-year sealed lithium battery single-station units, and carbon monoxide alarms within 10 feet of sleeping areas.
  • A portable fire extinguisher rated at least 2A-10B:C within 10 feet of the kitchen, mounted no higher than 5 feet, and tagged or receipted within the last 12 months.
  • Ground-fault outlets in kitchens, baths and outdoors, and at least two receptacles per bedroom.
  • Sound handrails, stairs, roofs, windows with screens, and working heating equipment.
  • No double-keyed deadbolts, which the form calls illegal.
  • All open permits closed out, and a well water certificate where a well serves the house.

Some repairs may need Uniform Construction Code permits, so call the office before hiring a contractor.

What if the Ewing house is a rental?

Rental houses carry extra paperwork in Ewing, and the registration status should be settled before a sale. Under township ordinance 10-07, residential rentals must be registered every year regardless of tenant changes, with the registration and rental fire prevention forms due January 31. Landlords also need a property maintenance inspection whenever a tenant changes.

If you sell a rental, give the buyer the registration record, the latest fire prevention form and any open violation notices. A buyer who wants to occupy the house will need the unit vacated on a schedule written into the contract.

What are the closing costs and recording steps in Ewing?

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee, and the deed is recorded with the Mercer County Clerk in Trenton, whose office has kept property records since 1838. For total consideration of $350,000 or less, the state schedule runs $2.00 per $500 up to $150,000, $3.35 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 per $500 from $200,000 to $350,000. Ask the closing attorney for the final figure.

The county charges $43 for the first page of a regular deed and $10 for each additional page. Realty transfer fees must be paid by cash, cashier's check, money order, attorney trust account or business escrow account, and amounts over $10,000 by certified or bank check. Mercer's land records page also notes that the transfer fee on sales of $1 million and above, often called the mansion tax, changed on July 10, 2025 so that the seller pays it.

New Jersey residents sign a GIT/REP-3 at closing. A nonresident owner owes an estimated payment of at least 2 percent of the price unless an exemption applies.

Is an inspection required to sell a house in Ewing?

Yes. The Division of Housing must inspect and approve every dwelling offered for resale in the township. The residential fee on the 2025 form is $125, and requests go through the SDL portal or the Construction Office at 609-883-2900, extension 7676.

What alarms does a Ewing resale inspection require?

The township asks for smoke alarms on every level, using ten-year sealed lithium battery single-station units, and carbon monoxide alarms within 10 feet of sleeping areas. It also asks for a labeled fire extinguisher near the kitchen that is tagged or receipted within 12 months.

How much does the Mercer County Clerk charge to record a deed?

A regular deed costs $43 for the first page and $10 for each added page. The state transfer fee is paid separately at recording and is set by the sale price. The county clerk accepts cash, cashier's check, money order, attorney trust account or business escrow account for that fee.

Do I have to register a rental before selling it in Ewing?

Registration is a yearly requirement under ordinance 10-07, with forms due January 31, so it should already be on file. Landlords also need a property maintenance inspection on each tenant change. Bring the paperwork to the sale so the buyer sees a clean record.

Can I sell a Ewing house with open permits?

Open permits must be closed out before the resale inspection can be passed, according to the township's inspection list. Call the Construction Office to learn what final inspections are outstanding. Some repairs also need new Uniform Construction Code permits before work begins.

What should I know before selling a house in Edison, NJ?

Edison is a Middlesex County township of about 30 square miles where the sale usually hinges on one local document, the Residential Resale Certificate, plus a state smoke certificate that has to come first. Nothing about those steps is hard, but each has lead time, so start them as soon as a buyer signs a contract.

The Census Bureau counts 109,077 residents for 2025 and 38,098 households. Roughly 61 percent of homes are owner occupied, and owners report a median home value of $496,900 for 2020 to 2024. Median household income is $125,145, and 47.7 percent of residents were born abroad.

How did Edison get its name, and why does it matter to a seller?

The township carries the inventor's name because voters changed it in 1954, and it sits on the ground where Thomas Edison ran his Menlo Park laboratory from 1876. The place was earlier called Raritan Township and was carved out of Piscataway and Woodbridge. Colonial-era buildings still stand near Piscatawaytown in South Edison, and three are listed nationally: the Laing House, the Benjamin Shotwell House and the Homestead Farm at Oak Ridge.

The township has many named sections, among them Stelton, Menlo Park, Oak Tree, Raritan Manor, Clara Barton, Lindenau and Washington Park. A house that has changed hands more than once is more likely to carry a finished basement, deck or addition from an earlier owner, and those are the items the township inspector checks for permits.

What does the Edison resale certificate require?

Edison Township Ordinance 14-1.6 says a Certificate for Change of Ownership must be obtained before the property closes, and the township form warns of fines up to $2,000 for skipping it. The application fee is $150, paid by certified check, credit card or money order. The form says no cash, no personal checks and no refunds. Code Enforcement takes the application by email at the resale address printed on the form and then calls for a card payment.

Timing is the part that trips people up. One line of the form asks for the inspection at least four weeks before the closing date, and another says three weeks, so plan on four. A smoke certificate must already exist before the resale certificate can be issued, and the inspector wants a copy on site.

What if work was done on the house without a permit?

  • The form says the current owner must resolve it, even if a previous owner did the work.
  • You pull a compliance permit, have the work inspected and close the permit before the certificate is issued.
  • Before the inspection, check the Building Department for open permits and ask the Tax Assessor whether improvements such as a finished basement are on the township record.
  • The ordinance covers every change of ownership, so a sale to a cash buyer still needs the certificate before closing.

Open permits are the most common reason an Edison closing slips. Ask the Building Department for a permit history on the address as soon as you list.

What does Edison look like to a buyer?

Edison surrounds the borough of Metuchen and touches East Brunswick, Highland Park, New Brunswick, Piscataway, Sayreville, South Plainfield and Woodbridge in Middlesex County, plus Clark, Plainfield and Scotch Plains in Union County. The township sits roughly 27 miles from both Midtown Manhattan and Trenton.

  • Rail: Edison station in South Edison runs NJ Transit Northeast Corridor trains to Newark Penn, New York Penn and Trenton, and North Edison residents may be closer to Metropark or Metuchen stations.
  • Roads: Route 27, Route 440, U.S. Route 1, Interstate 287 and about five miles of the New Jersey Turnpike, with Exit 10 inside the township.
  • Jobs: Raritan Center, a 2,300 acre business park, plus the state's largest private convention center, warehouse hubs and an Amazon fulfillment center.

Census workers here spend 33.9 minutes getting to their jobs on average.

How does Edison's weather show up in a home inspection?

The township's climate is humid subtropical, and rain and melted snow add up to about 49.6 inches a year, the wettest stretch running through late summer, and snow falls several times each winter. Recorded extremes run from minus 17 degrees in 1934 to 106 degrees in 1936 and 1949.

A buyer's inspector will therefore look closely at the roof, gutters and basement walls, and the township checklist adds the water heater and stair rails. Fixing a damp basement corner or a loose guardrail before you list costs less than negotiating it after the inspection report.

Which schools serve Edison homes?

Edison Township Public Schools serve pre-kindergarten through grade 12 and split the township between two high schools. Homes in the south feed Edison High School, and homes in the north feed J.P. Stevens High School. The district reported 16,268 students across 19 schools for 2021-22. Families also look at the Greater Brunswick Charter School and the Middlesex County Magnet Schools, which accept applications from eighth graders countywide.

When you list, name the attendance zone for the street you are on. The zone is part of how a listing is described.

How do property tax appeals and closing costs work for an Edison seller?

Property tax appeals go to the Middlesex County Board of Taxation, which has said it will not hold virtual hearings. The state deadline is April 1, moved to May 1 where a municipality has done a revaluation.

At closing the seller pays the state realty transfer fee. The state's own example shows $1,910 on a $325,000 deed with no exemption. Edison sellers who live in New Jersey sign GIT/REP-3 to record the deed, while nonresident sellers use GIT/REP-1 or GIT/REP-2 unless they qualify under a seller's assurance.

Where does the deed get recorded in Edison?

The Middlesex County Clerk records every deed for Edison at the County Administration Building, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick. The office takes walk-ins on weekdays, opening at 8:30 and closing at 4:10, with a 4:00 arrival cutoff. Paper filings need a cover sheet, and skipping it adds a $20 indexing charge. The deed must say "Prepared by," list tax block, lot and consideration, and carry a return address.

Most Edison closings go through an attorney or title company that records electronically, so this matters mainly when you sell without one.

More questions about Edison, NJ

How much does the Edison resale certificate cost?

The township form lists a $150 fee. It must be paid by certified check, credit card or money order, and the form states there are no cash payments, no personal checks and no refunds. Fines of up to $2,000 apply if you close without the certificate.

Do I need the smoke certificate before the Edison inspection?

Yes. The form says the smoke certificate is required before the resale certificate can be issued. If the Fire Prevention inspection happens first, give the inspector a copy at the resale visit or email it to the township's resale address.

Can I sell an Edison house with a finished basement that has no permit?

You can sell it, but the certificate will not issue until a permit is obtained, the work passes inspection and the permit is closed. Check with the Building Department and the Tax Assessor before you schedule the inspection.

Which county office records an Edison deed?

The Middlesex County Clerk in New Brunswick. The office is open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. and requires arrival by 4:00 p.m., and paper documents need a cover sheet.

What is the deadline to appeal an Edison property tax assessment?

April 1 of the tax year, or May 1 when the township completed a revaluation. File with the Middlesex County Board of Taxation. Properties assessed above $1,000,000 can go straight to the State Tax Court.

How can you sell a house fast in Howell, New Jersey?

Howell sellers can hire an agent, go it alone or take a cash purchase. All three meet the township's fire inspection, the one local step nobody skips. Howell is a large, mostly single-family township in Monmouth County, so many sellers have a detached house on a sizeable lot, sometimes with older systems.

  • Agent listing: exposure to the most buyers, which suits a house that shows well, though appraisals, mortgage approval and repair requests stretch the calendar.
  • Private sale: you skip the commission and handle the price, the contract and the alarm inspection yourself.
  • Cash buyer: no lender and no repair haggling, which fits an inherited home, a vacant house or a short move deadline.

Under any of them, book the Fire Bureau inspection early. Failing it for a missing detector is the most avoidable delay in a Howell sale.

Where is Howell Township and how did it grow?

At roughly 61.21 square miles, Howell is Monmouth County's biggest municipality by area, and 60.27 of those miles are land. It borders Colts Neck, Freehold Township and Wall in Monmouth County and Brick, Jackson and Lakewood in Ocean County. Named communities inside the township include Ramtown, Adelphia, Ardena, Land of Pines, Southard and Squankum.

The Legislature carved Howell out of Shrewsbury Township on February 23, 1801. Brick split off in 1850 and Wall in 1851, and Farmingdale became its own borough in 1903. Because the township still surrounds Farmingdale completely, it is one of the state's 21 pairs of doughnut towns.

The area was once iron country. Bog iron fed the Howell Works in the 19th century, and the preserved Allaire Village now sits inside Allaire State Park along the Howell and Wall border. The ground is sandy Outer Coastal Plain soil with pine and oak woods, wetlands and the 1,204 acre Manasquan Reservoir nearby.

What do Census figures show about housing in Howell?

Howell is firmly a township of owners: QuickFacts puts owner occupancy at 88.8 percent, the highest of the four places in its comparison table. The median owned home is valued at $507,200. Typical monthly costs are $2,846 for owners with a mortgage and $1,133 for those without.

Households number 19,134, each with 2.81 people on average, and median household income is $134,854. The poverty rate is 6.8 percent. Retail sales came to $23,830 per resident in 2022, far above the other three places in the same table, and shopping centers line Route 9. The 2020 count was 53,537 people, and the estimate for July 2025 is 55,156.

Residents 65 and older make up 17.2 percent of the township, and 89.3 percent of people stayed at one address through the prior year. A house needing work still sells, and a buyer who accepts its condition shortens the path.

How do Howell residents get to work and school?

Most working residents leave the township. The state labor department places Howell in the Monmouth-Ocean labor area, and more than 70 percent of employed residents work outside it, per the township's encyclopedia entry. Health care and social assistance employs 16.3 percent, retail 13.8 percent and education 11.1 percent.

  • Roads: Interstate 195, U.S. 9, Route 33 and Route 34 all cross the township, plus County Routes 524, 547 and 549. The Garden State Parkway is reached from I-195 and Route 33 at exits 98 and 100.
  • Buses: NJ Transit routes 131, 135 and 139 head to the Port Authority Bus Terminal. Resident-only park-and-ride lots sit at Aldrich, in Land of Pines, and in Adelphia. Belmar is the nearest train station.
  • Schools: the Howell Township district serves pre-kindergarten through grade 8 in 12 schools with 6,045 students in 2024-25. High schoolers attend Howell, Freehold Township or Colts Neck High School in the Freehold Regional district depending on address.

Horse farms and nurseries remain part of the landscape, which is why rural lots and acreage show up in local listings.

What does the Howell Fire Bureau require before a house changes hands?

Howell uses a Certificate of Smoke Alarm, Carbon Monoxide Alarm and Secondary Power Source Compliance for resales, handled by the Fire Bureau at 4567 Highway 9 North, second floor. Clean and test every alarm before the inspector arrives. The required type depends on when the house was built or renovated.

Smoke alarm minimums by construction date, from the Howell Fire Bureau compliance requirements sheet
Built or renovatedMinimum alarms
Before 197710 year sealed battery alarms on all levels
January 1977 to September 1978Electric alarm on each sleeping level, sealed battery elsewhere
October 1978 to January 1983Electric on sleeping level and basement, sealed battery elsewhere
February 1983 to July 1984Electric alarms on all levels
August 1984 to February 1991Electric on all levels, interconnected
March 1991 onwardElectric on every level and in each bedroom, interconnected, with battery backup

The sheet adds more details sellers miss.

  • Alarms must be under 10 years old by manufacture date, and replacing electric alarms with battery models is not allowed.
  • One and two family homes with a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage need carbon monoxide alarms on each sleeping level and near every bedroom door.
  • A solar array, generator or battery system calls for a printed label reading CAUTION: MULTIPLE SOURCES OF POWER within 18 inches of the main panel and the meter.
  • House numbers must be at least 4 inches tall, contrast with the background and be visible from the street.
  • The sheet drops the old extinguisher rule for one and two family homes that change hands.

The Fire Bureau's number is 732-938-4500, extension 2900.

How do Howell property tax appeals and payoffs work?

Monmouth County follows a different calendar from most of New Jersey, so a Howell appeal is due January 15 rather than April 1. The state's appeals page lists Monmouth County alongside Burlington and Gloucester, and gives the Monmouth County Board of Taxation number as 732-431-7404. Appeals are filed on Form A-1 with that board.

If the board's judgment disappoints you, the Tax Court of New Jersey must receive your appeal within 45 days of that judgment. Owners of property assessed over $1,000,000 can skip the board and file with the Tax Court.

The township forms page lists Tax Collector requests for lien redemption figures, bank code removal and prepaid taxes. Ask for a redemption figure early if the house has a tax lien, since the payoff has to be in the closing statement.

Who records a Howell deed and what do the state rules add?

Deeds for a Howell sale are recorded by the Monmouth County Clerk, whose site lists real property recordings, e-recording and a recording fee schedule. Your title company normally files the deed and the tax forms together.

The seller pays the State Realty Transfer Fee. A sale at Howell's median value of $507,200 lands in the over-$350,000 schedule, where $4.80 per $500 applies between $200,000 and $550,000. Sellers who remain in the state sign GIT/REP-3. Someone relocating out of New Jersey becomes a nonresident for tax purposes on this sale, and an estimated payment of 2 percent of the price or 8.97 percent of the gain may come due at the table unless an exemption covers it.

More questions about Howell, NJ

What inspection does Howell require before I sell?

A smoke alarm, carbon monoxide alarm and secondary power source compliance inspection by the Howell Fire Bureau. The alarm type required depends on the year the house was built or renovated. Test and clean the alarms first, then confirm the appointment with the bureau at 732-938-4500, extension 2900.

Do I need fire extinguishers to sell a Howell home?

No, for a one or two family dwelling. According to the Fire Bureau's sheet, extinguishers no longer come into play when ownership or occupancy changes in those homes and in attached single-family units. Alarms, carbon monoxide detectors and any power-source label do still need to pass.

When is the deadline to appeal a Howell tax assessment?

January 15, because Monmouth County follows an alternative assessment calendar. Most other New Jersey counties use April 1. File Form A-1 with the Monmouth County Board of Taxation, and call that office at 732-431-7404 if you are unsure which date applies to your parcel.

Which county office records the deed on a Howell sale?

The Monmouth County Clerk. The office handles real property recordings and e-recording, and its website carries the recording fee schedule. Closing is where the deed, the transfer fee affidavit and the GIT/REP form usually get bundled and sent in by the title agent.

Can I sell a Howell house with tenants in it?

Yes. The township keeps rental forms, including a combined rental certificate, a landlord registration for multi-unit property and a single unit rental application. Pull those filings and the current lease before you list, since buyers on either side will want to see the terms.

What is it like to sell a house in Barnegat Township?

Barnegat Township in Ocean County is a fast-growing, mostly owner-occupied community where sellers deal with a township resale letter, a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate and, in many cases, environmental approvals tied to the location of the lot. It covers about 34 square miles of land between the Garden State Parkway corridor and Barnegat Bay.

Because nearly nine in ten homes are owner-occupied, most sales here are between households rather than investors. The sections below cover the local numbers, the township paperwork and the county steps that follow a signed contract.

How has Barnegat grown, and what do the housing numbers show?

The township reached 24,296 residents in the 2020 census, up from 20,936 in 2010, and the Census Bureau estimates 26,151 by mid-2025. That is a 7.6% rise over the estimate base for April 2020. Wikipedia notes that the 2020 count was the highest in the township's history.

Where is Barnegat, and what shapes its history and layout?

Barnegat is a township in Ocean County, incorporated in 1846 as Union Township from parts of Dover and Stafford, and renamed Barnegat Township effective January 1, 1977. The name traces to Dutch explorers who mapped Barnegat Inlet in 1614, and the early spelling is usually translated as "inlet of the breakers."

The township includes the Barnegat census-designated place, part of Ocean Acres, which it shares with Stafford Township, and smaller localities such as Cedar Bridge, Howardsville, Lower Dock and Upper Dock. Barnegat borders Lacey, Little Egg Harbor, Long Beach, Ocean and Stafford townships in Ocean County, plus Bass River and Woodland townships in Burlington County. The Battle of Cedar Bridge, a skirmish near the Cedar Bridge Tavern in 1782, is one of the township's best-known historical events.

Which roads and schools matter to Barnegat buyers?

The Garden State Parkway runs north to south near the middle of the township, and U.S. Route 9 runs through the eastern side. New Jersey Route 72 and County Route 539 serve the western part, while County Route 554 crosses the township west to east. NJ Transit bus route 559 connects the area with Atlantic City, and the census puts the average commute at 27.8 minutes.

Public school students attend the Barnegat Township School District, which Wikipedia lists with six schools and 3,583 students in 2021-22. Include the district name and your bus or school-zone details in your listing, since buyers with children ask first.

  • Route 9 and Route 72 frontage can trigger state highway approvals for work on the lot.
  • About 31% of residents are 65 or older, which keeps single-level homes and low-maintenance lots in demand.

What paperwork does Barnegat Township require for a home sale?

Barnegat Township requires a Letter of No Interest on resales, according to the Code Enforcement page, and the Forms page lists a Resale Complete Letter of No Interest and a state smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification. Call the township's Rentals and Resales line at 609-698-0080, extension 159, before you list.

The township's construction office also handles permit history, which matters if you finished a basement, built a deck or added a shed. Unpermitted work can slow a sale, so ask the office whether your permits were closed. The township routes calls by extension on the same main line: construction permits at 135, 150 and 153, the planning and zoning board at 155, and the fire, electrical and plumbing subcodes at 157, 158 and 115. Having the right extension saves a round of transfers when a buyer's inspector asks for sign-offs.

  • Zoning permits cover sheds, fences, decks, pools, driveways, patios and additions.
  • A fence needs a zoning permit and a survey or plot plan from a licensed New Jersey surveyor.
  • Tree clearing permits are required before cutting trees.
  • Vacant properties must be registered with the township, and the forms page carries both registration and de-registration forms.

Do Pinelands, DEP or septic rules affect a sale in Barnegat?

They can, depending on where the lot sits. The township's construction office lists the prior approvals that come before local permits: Pinelands approval for land west of the Parkway only, state environmental approval for waterfront and freshwater wetland areas, and Department of Transportation approval for Route 9 and Route 72 properties.

The same page lists county health department approval for septic systems, wells and food handling, and county soil conservation district review for soil disturbance of 5,000 square feet or more. If your house is on septic, ask a buyer's inspector which records they will want. If part of your lot lies west of the Parkway, tell your agent early so buyers understand what Pinelands rules may mean for later projects.

What if I rent the house or my buyer is a senior?

Rental properties in Barnegat need a certificate of occupancy before every new tenant and must be registered with the municipal clerk. Units rented for fewer than 30 days need a yearly certificate, and failure to file can bring a summons to the owner.

On the state side, New Jersey publishes a reduced realty transfer fee schedule for senior citizens, blind or disabled persons, and for low and moderate income housing. The standard sale above $350,000 starts at $2.90 per $500 for the first $150,000, while the reduced schedule starts at $1.40. Ask your closing agent whether the transaction qualifies. The township's forms page also lists affordable housing applications for purchase and rental, which matters if your house sits in a program.

Where is the deed recorded and who pays the transfer fees?

Deeds for Barnegat sales are recorded with the Ocean County Clerk, whose office handles land records and property search for the county. The seller pays the state realty transfer fee when the deed goes on record, and a seller who lives out of state also files a GIT/REP form and prepays at least 2% of the deed consideration.

Plan for these items on closing day: the payoff of any mortgage, the transfer fee, township certificate costs and any unpaid taxes or water and sewer charges. A cash buyer or a title company can walk through those lines before you sign.

Does Barnegat Township require anything special to sell a house?

Yes. The township asks for a Letter of No Interest on resales, and sellers also need the state smoke and carbon monoxide certification. Call the Rentals and Resales line at 609-698-0080, extension 159, to confirm current steps.

Is Barnegat mostly owner-occupied?

Yes. The Census Bureau reports an 88.0% owner-occupied rate for 2020-2024, with a median home value of $399,000, so most sales are between homeowners.

Do Pinelands rules apply to every Barnegat property?

No. The township lists Pinelands approval for land west of the Garden State Parkway only. Lots east of the Parkway may still need state environmental approval if they are on the water or near wetlands.

Which roads serve Barnegat Township?

The Garden State Parkway crosses the middle of the township, and U.S. Route 9 runs through the east. Route 72 and County Route 539 serve the west, and County Route 554 crosses west to east.

Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Barnegat sale?

The seller does. The state sets the fee by sale price in steps per $500, the county clerk collects it with the deed, and seniors may qualify for a reduced schedule.

What are the quickest ways to sell in Brick Township?

A seller in Brick has three realistic paths: hire an agent, handle the sale alone, or sign with a cash buyer who purchases the property untouched. Cash moves fastest and generally pays least. Listing adds commission and fix-up costs and takes longer. The right choice turns on the roof, the flood history, your deadline, and what the house would net after each route.

Ocean County's Brick Township was estimated at 77,402 people in mid-2025, up 5.1% from the 2020 base, per the Census Bureau. That growth, in a place that lost population between 2000 and 2020, means buyers are active, but the housing stock is mostly decades old. Many sellers meet the same questions: flood zones, inspection paperwork, and quarterly tax bills.

What kind of housing market is Brick Township?

Brick is a mature shore suburb where owners dominate. The 2020-2024 survey counts 30,289 households, 82.2% of them owning, with a $410,600 median home value and $106,130 median income. Rent runs $1,756 a month at the median, so a rental is a realistic fallback for some owners but not a cheap one to maintain under the township's inspection rules.

The township covers 25.59 square miles of land plus a lot of water. The mainland sits along the Metedeconk River and Barnegat Bay, and a separate set of ocean beaches (Brick Ocean Beaches I, II and III) lies on the barrier peninsula. Because the two parts do not touch, a street address can mean very different insurance and elevation questions. Older neighborhoods such as Laurelton, Lake Riviera and Baywood grew after the Garden State Parkway opened in 1954 and a building boom ran through the 1980s.

  • Many homes date from the 1950s through the 1980s, so roofs, septic or sewer connections, and electrical panels are common negotiation points.
  • Waterfront and bayfront lots near Cherry Quay, Havens Cove and Shore Acres carry their own flood and elevation questions.
  • Herbertsville and Parkway Pines sit near Parkway exit 91, away from the rest of the township, and attract commuters.

How does flood risk change a Brick home sale?

Flood history is the single biggest local variable. Hurricane Sandy in October 2012 devastated parts of Brick, and barrier island and waterfront properties took the worst of it; some buildings had to be torn down. A February 2026 blizzard also dropped roughly two feet of snow and knocked out power in several areas, which is a reminder that roofs and heating systems matter even away from the water.

The township's floodplain information page says it provides flood zone data to realtors, lenders, insurers and owners, including base flood elevation, whether a lot is in a coastal barrier area, and whether flood insurance is mandatory. Elevation certificates on file can be searched through the township's mapping tool, or requested from the engineering office by address or block and lot. Pull the certificate before you list, because a buyer's lender will ask for it.

Brick takes part in the federal Community Rating System, which can lower flood premiums. Its floodplain plan lists 140 mitigation initiatives, 81 of them completed by the latest annual report. A seller who can show an elevation certificate, a recent flood policy, and any raised-utility work usually faces fewer price cuts.

Which schools and roads do Brick buyers ask about?

Brick Public Schools serves pre-kindergarten through grade 12 inside the township. The district ran 12 schools and about 8,414 students in 2020-21, with elementary schools such as Drum Point, Lanes Mill, Midstreams, Osbornville, Veterans Memorial and Emma Havens Young, two middle schools (Lake Riviera and Veterans Memorial), and two high schools: Brick Memorial and Brick Township High School. Buyers often check which elementary zone a street falls in, so mention it in the listing.

The Garden State Parkway crosses the western side with exits 89, 90 and 91. Routes 70, 88 and 35 and county routes 528 and 549 handle local traffic. The old Laurelton Circle at Routes 70 and 88 once carried about 95,000 vehicles a day before it became a signal-controlled intersection in 1986. NJ Transit runs the 137 bus to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Manhattan and the 67 to Newark, and a Park and Ride at exit 91 serves express commuters. Average commute time for workers is 28.2 minutes.

What township paperwork applies when a Brick house is sold or rented?

Brick's Division of Inspections, which is the Building Department, issues construction permits and handles requests for certificates under the New Jersey Uniform Construction Code. Open or unclosed permits are the usual cause of delay at closing, so have the division confirm the status of past work before you sign. The building office answers permit and certificate questions by voicemail and email, listed in the table below.

Brick also treats rental homes strictly. Owners must register the landlord with the clerk, apply for a Rental Certificate of Occupancy, and file a mercantile license with proof of at least $500,000 in liability coverage. Code Enforcement then inspects every rental each year, at $100 per inspection and $50 per failed re-inspection. The annual checklist covers smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, ground-fault outlets near water, a mounted fire extinguisher, and lead-safe status for structures built before 1978. Since September 27, 2022, creditors must also register foreclosed or vacant residential and commercial properties with the township within 10 days of filing a foreclosure action.

How are Brick property taxes billed, and what happens at closing?

Brick's tax year follows the calendar, with installments falling on the first of February, May, August and November and a ten-day grace window after each. Each bill covers a calendar quarter (the February bill pays for January through March), which matters at closing because the seller owes tax only through the closing date. A missing bill is no defense against interest, the tax collector warns, so make sure the closing agent has the current quarter's figure.

Work done on the house can add a second layer. After construction is finished, the township places an assessment on the improvement and mails an Added Assessment Bill in October, due November 1 and again on February 1 and May 1 of the following year. A seller who finished a deck or addition should ask the assessor whether that bill is still coming.

  • Assessment notices go out each year, usually by February 1, and an owner who thinks the value is wrong may appeal on or before April 1 to the Ocean County Board of Taxation.
  • Properties assessed above $1,000,000 can file directly with the State Tax Court of New Jersey.
  • The assessor processes veteran and senior or disabled deductions, each currently $250.

What does New Jersey charge a seller on a house sale?

The state's Realty Transfer Fee is the seller's cost, collected as the deed goes on record. On a standard sale of $350,000 or less, the rate is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 on the next $50,000, and $3.90 on the remainder. Above $350,000 the schedule starts at $2.90 and climbs to $4.80 per $500 between $200,000 and $550,000. At Brick's median value of roughly $410,600, most sales land in that second schedule. For the exact figure on your price, use the Division of Taxation rate tables.

Closing costs also include deed recording, any payoff of liens, and whatever the buyer negotiates for repairs. A cash buyer typically absorbs repairs, so the realistic comparison is your net after repairs, carrying costs through the winter, and agent fees against a single offer with a closing date you choose.

Is a cash sale the right call for a Brick homeowner?

A cash sale fits best when the home has defects an inspector would flag, when flood or storm damage is unrepaired, when the owner has inherited a house in another town, or when quarterly tax bills and a mortgage are piling up. It also helps landlords who do not want to carry the annual rental inspection cycle. It makes less sense for a move-in-ready home on a good street where a listing will draw several offers.

Whatever the buyer, get the offer on paper, set it beside the proceeds of a listing after commission, and confirm who pays for the certificate and recording steps. If you are close to a foreclosure filing, speak to a housing counselor or attorney in addition to any buyer, because the township's vacant property registration and the lender's timeline both affect your options.

More questions about Brick, NJ

Can I sell my Brick house if it was damaged in a storm?

Yes. Houses with storm damage change hands regularly, mostly to investors and cash buyers who subtract the repair bill. Collect your elevation certificate, flood claim paperwork and permit history first. The engineering office can look up certificates by address or by block and lot.

Which Brick office handles permits and certificates?

Start with the Division of Inspections voicemail line, 732-262-4604, or the permit status email on the township's building page. Rental certificate matters belong to Code Enforcement, 732-262-1033, weekdays.

What is the cutoff for contesting a Brick assessment?

April 1 each year, filed with the Ocean County Board of Taxation. Owners of property assessed above $1,000,000 may file directly with the State Tax Court of New Jersey instead.

Does a landlord need a certificate before selling a rented house in Brick?

A landlord needs the Rental Certificate of Occupancy to keep tenants in place, and the township inspects each rental every year. Ask the Division of Inspections what is required for your property when the sale closes and whether tenants move out first.

Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Brick sale?

The seller pays it. Recording the deed triggers the charge, which follows the price written in the deed and the Division of Taxation's published rates. Sales above $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee.

What are the fastest ways to sell in Bridgewater Township?

An owner in a hurry can accept a cash offer, hire a listing agent, or find a buyer without one. In this township the listing route is strong, because prices are high and buyers are plentiful, so people pick cash for other reasons: a house in need of work, a relocation date, an estate, or a landlord leaving the business.

Bridgewater Township sits in the middle of Somerset County in the Raritan Valley, about 32 miles from Manhattan. The Census Bureau estimates 46,455 residents on July 1, 2025, up 1.0% from the 2020 base, which makes it the county's second-largest municipality after Franklin Township.

What does the Bridgewater housing market look like?

Bridgewater is among the pricier towns in central New Jersey. Census figures for 2020 to 2024 show a median owner-occupied value of $605,500, an owner-occupied rate of 84.9%, median household income of $172,851, and median gross rent of $2,176. About 16,505 households average 2.75 people, and 61.8% of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree. Median owner costs with a mortgage run $3,258 a month, so buyers are sensitive to taxes and condition.

The township spreads over 31.89 land square miles and mixes older neighborhoods with large newer developments. It is split into recognized sections without formal borders:

  • Bradley Gardens, an older southwestern area with newer pockets and a commercial strip on Old York Road.
  • Green Knoll, the central area with Bridgewater Commons, the municipal building and the high school.
  • Finderne, in the southeast, with older streets, newer developments and TD Bank Ballpark, home to the Somerset Patriots.
  • Martinsville, the largest census-designated place at 12,147 residents in 2020, and Bridgewater Center in the west.

How do jobs, commuting and shopping affect Bridgewater buyers?

Bridgewater is the commercial hub of Somerset County. Pharmaceutical and life-science employers anchor the economy, with Sanofi's U.S. headquarters in the township, and Bridgewater Commons, a mall of roughly 994,000 square feet anchored by Bloomingdale's and Macy's, draws shoppers from several counties. The Census lists average travel time to work at 31.4 minutes, which fits a place where many residents commute out and many workers commute in.

Interstate 287 is the main limited-access road, Interstate 78 passes through the north without exits, and U.S. 22, Route 28 and Routes 202-206 cross the township. The Raritan Valley Line stops at Bridgewater station, and NJ Transit buses run to the Port Authority Bus Terminal (route 114) and Newark (route 65). Newark Liberty Airport is about 25 miles away. Buyers moving from New York or north Jersey often ask which streets are closest to the station and the highways, so put that in the listing.

Which schools serve Bridgewater homes?

Most of the township is in the Bridgewater-Raritan Regional School District, the largest in Somerset County, which also serves the borough of Raritan. It operated 11 schools and 8,254 students in 2020-21. The primary schools are Adamsville, Bradley Gardens, Crim, Hamilton, John F. Kennedy (in Raritan), Milltown and Van Holten; Eisenhower and Hillside are intermediate schools for grades 5 and 6; Bridgewater-Raritan Middle School covers grades 7 and 8; and Bridgewater-Raritan High School serves grades 9 through 12.

The township is also home to the Somerset County Vocational and Technical High School, a county magnet school, and the headquarters of the Somerset County Library System. Because buyers often shop by elementary zone, confirm the primary school for your street with the district before you advertise it.

What does Bridgewater require before you renovate or sell?

The township's Code Enforcement office administers construction permits and issues certificates of approval and occupancy after final inspection. A permit is generally needed for decks, pools, additions, garages, finishing a basement, new electrical outlets, and new or replacement furnaces, water heaters or air conditioning. A shed needs one if it is over 200 square feet or has utilities, a fence only if it is over 6 feet or serves as a pool barrier, and roofing only where sheathing is replaced. State law lets the construction official fine unpermitted work up to $2,000 per violation, which is why open or missing permits surface during a buyer's review. Plan review can take up to 20 working days.

Home fire safety requirements and applications are handled by the township's Fire Safety office. Call the main line at 908-725-6300, extension 5560 for construction questions and extension 5550 for fire safety, to confirm what a buyer's inspection will check. The municipal offices are at 100 Commons Way.

How are Bridgewater property taxes billed and appealed?

Bridgewater bills in four installments. The tax collector lists due dates of February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a ten-day grace period. If the lender escrows your taxes, the lender must supply the correct bank code to the tax office, and when a mortgage is paid off at closing the office should be told to remove it. The assessor runs an annual reassessment program, and each property must be inspected on a four-year cycle, so a visit from the township's appraisal contractor before a sale is not unusual.

Source: Bridgewater Township Tax Assessor and Tax Collector pages.

What does the state charge on a higher-priced Bridgewater sale?

With a median value above $600,000, many Bridgewater sales exceed the thresholds in New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee schedule. The seller pays at recording. For deals above $350,000 the rate per $500 of price runs $2.90 on the first $150,000, $4.25 up to $200,000, $4.80 up to $550,000 and $5.30 from $550,000 to $850,000.

When the price tops $1,000,000 for a residential property, a supplemental Graduated Percent Fee applies and the seller is responsible for it: 1% for sales up to $2,000,000, 2% up to $2,500,000, 2.5% up to $3,000,000, 3% up to $3,500,000 and 3.5% above that. The Division of Taxation posts the exemptions and forms, including RTF-1EE, on its realty transfer fee page. A cash buyer's lower price should be compared against these fees plus commission, not just the headline number.

What flood and site issues come up in Bridgewater?

The Raritan River forms much of the southern edge, and the North Branch of the Raritan marks the western border. In August 2011, Hurricane Irene submerged the former American Cyanamid Superfund site, about 560 acres of which lie in the township, and chemicals leaked into the river. If your home is low-lying near the river, ask the township engineering office about flood information before you list, and keep any flood insurance and repair records for the buyer. The northeastern part, by contrast, is hilly because the First Watchung Mountain runs through it.

More questions about Bridgewater, NJ

When are Bridgewater property taxes due?

February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, each with a ten-day grace period. A tenth day that lands on a weekend or holiday moves the cutoff to the next business day.

When must a Bridgewater assessment appeal be filed?

The township's assessor page lists May 1 of the tax year as the appeal due date. Confirm the date against the notice you receive from the Tax Assessor at 908-725-6300, extension 5121.

Does a Bridgewater shed or fence need a permit?

Only in some cases. A shed needs a permit if it is over 200 square feet or has electric or plumbing, and a fence needs one if it is over 6 feet tall or serves as a pool barrier.

Which school district covers Bridgewater?

The Bridgewater-Raritan Regional School District, which covers pre-kindergarten through grade 12 for Bridgewater and the borough of Raritan. The district reported 11 schools in the 2020-21 school year.

Does a sale above $1,000,000 cost more in New Jersey?

Yes. Residential sales above $1,000,000 carry a Graduated Percent Fee on top of the Realty Transfer Fee, starting at 1% of total consideration, and the seller is responsible for it.

How do you sell a house fast in Hillsborough, New Jersey?

A seller here has three practical paths: an agent's listing, a sale without an agent, or a buyer who pays cash and takes the house in its present condition. The township is in Somerset County, in the Raritan Valley, and its own website describes it as 52 miles from Manhattan.

Speed in Hillsborough depends less on the price you pick than on the paperwork. A smoke detector certificate, any open building permits and a clean tax record decide how soon a closing date can be set.

  • Agent listing: the widest exposure, but showings, a buyer's mortgage and a repair list all add weeks.
  • Without an agent: the commission stays with you, along with the pricing, the contract and the arrangements for the township's alarm inspection.
  • Cash buyer: no lender and no repair negotiation, so the timeline is mostly the title work and the certificate inspection.

Weigh each path by the dollars left after fees and repairs.

Where is Hillsborough and how did it develop?

Hillsborough Township covers 55.10 square miles, which makes it the largest of Somerset County's 21 municipalities by area. Its 54.61 square miles of land include several named communities, among them Belle Mead, Neshanic, Flagtown, Amwell and Woods Tavern.

A royal charter created the township in September 1771, and the Legislature incorporated it on February 21, 1798. Millstone split off as a borough in 1894 and Manville in 1929. Growth came mostly after 1950: the population went from 3,875 that year to 36,634 in 2000 and 43,276 in the 2020 census, according to the encyclopedia entry on the township.

Nearly 40 percent of the land is protected or preserved open space. That includes Duke Farms, a 2,700 acre estate in the northeast corner, so a house near preserved land will often have farm or woodland views that stay put.

The climate is humid subtropical. January lows average 18 degrees and July highs reach 85. Annual precipitation of 47.85 inches puts roofs, gutters and basements on a buyer's inspection list.

What do Census figures say about Hillsborough homes and owners?

Owners live in 79.5 percent of Hillsborough's housing units, according to QuickFacts. An owned home has a median value of $547,600. At the median, owners carrying a mortgage spend $3,017 a month on housing and owners without one spend $1,470.

There are 16,388 households of about 2.67 people each, with median income of $154,031 and an average commute of 33.3 minutes. Turnover is low: 91.1 percent of residents were at the same address a year earlier. Population is estimated at 45,061 for July 2025, a 4.1 percent gain over the 2020 base.

For a seller this means your likely buyer is a commuter household with a sizable income, and a listing competes with a modest supply of similar homes. A buyer who needs cash certainty or no financing contingency is a smaller group but a real one.

Which roads, buses and schools do buyers weigh in Hillsborough?

Buyers here ask about the commute and the school district before they ask about the kitchen. The facts below come from the township's entry on the public encyclopedia.

  • Roads: U.S. Route 206 is the main route. A 3.75 mile bypass finished in 2021, and the old road is meant to become a downtown main street. County Routes 514 and 533 also cross the township, while Interstate 287 sits just outside in Bridgewater and Franklin.
  • Transit: D.H.I.L.A.N. buses link to Manville, Bridgewater and Somerville, and Coach USA runs four weekday morning express trips to Midtown Manhattan. A proposed West Trenton rail line with Belle Mead and Hillsborough stops was cancelled for lack of funding.
  • Schools: the Hillsborough Township School District runs pre-kindergarten through grade 12. Its nine schools include five K to 4 elementaries, Auten Road Intermediate for grades 5 and 6, a middle school for 7 and 8 and the high school. Enrollment was 7,288 in 2020-21.

What paperwork does a Hillsborough seller handle before closing?

Four offices touch a Hillsborough sale: the Fire Safety Department, the Building Department, the Tax Collector and the Somerset County Clerk. The table lists what each one asks of the seller.

Hillsborough closing checklist, from the township Building and Tax pages and the Somerset County Clerk land records page
ItemOfficeWhat to know
Smoke detector certificationFire Safety DepartmentFor a resale, the Building Department does not issue a certificate of occupancy. Schedule this inspection instead.
Open permitsBuilding DepartmentThe current owner must close any open permit, even one pulled by a previous owner.
Quarterly taxesTax CollectorBilled on the first of February, May, August and November. Payment is on time through the 10th.
Deed recordingSomerset County ClerkA county cover sheet goes with every deed. The first page costs $45 and each added page $10.

The township's SDL portal shows permit status and inspection results, so pull the permit history for your address early. Fixing a stale permit takes less time than explaining it to a buyer's attorney.

How are Hillsborough property taxes billed and what happens when you sell?

The township mails an estimated third-quarter bill each July, based on the current year's assessed value. The Tax Collector warns against multiplying that bill by four, because adjustments land in the third and fourth quarters.

Hillsborough runs an annual reassessment program, so assessments follow market movement from year to year. Township figures show the rate falling from $2.419 per $100 of assessed value in 2018 to $2.143 in 2024, even as values climbed. A check mailed on the 9th but received on the 12th is late, because the office ignores postmarks.

If you pay by ACH direct debit, tell the Tax Collector as soon as you list. The office says debits continue until it is notified. A seller with unpaid taxes should request a payoff figure ahead of closing. The township's online auction of 2025 and prior delinquent charges ran from August 21 to September 23, 2026.

Assessment appeals go to the Somerset County Board of Taxation. The statewide date is April 1, pushed to May 1 in a district that has been revalued or reassessed, so confirm which one fits your parcel. If the board rules against you, the Tax Court takes a petition for 45 days after the ruling.

What does the state add to the cost of selling in Hillsborough?

Recording the deed triggers New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee, and the seller pays it. At the Hillsborough median value of $547,600 the schedule for sales above $350,000 applies, and the $4.80 per $500 band covers most of the price. The Division of Taxation publishes every band.

A seller who stays a New Jersey resident signs GIT/REP-3 at the table, so no income tax is estimated at closing. A home that was your main residence for two of the five years before sale may qualify for the gain exclusion that New Jersey follows: $250,000 for one filer, $500,000 for joint filers.

More questions about Hillsborough, NJ

Do I need a certificate of occupancy to sell my Hillsborough house?

Not from the Building Department, which says it issues none for a residential resale. The Fire Safety Department handles a smoke detector certification inspection, and that is the visit you book. Your closing attorney can say whether a buyer's lender wants anything more.

When are Hillsborough property taxes due?

On the first of February, May, August and November. A grace period runs through the 10th and extends to the next business day when the 10th lands on a weekend or holiday. After that, interest is charged back to the first, and a postmark does not rescue a late payment.

What is the deadline to appeal a Hillsborough assessment?

Usually April 1, on Form A-1 with the Somerset County Board of Taxation. Where a revaluation or reassessment has been carried out the date shifts to May 1. The board or the township assessor can tell you which one governs your parcel before you prepare the petition.

Who records the deed when I sell in Hillsborough?

The Somerset County Clerk, whose office files deeds, mortgages and related papers. Every filing needs a county cover sheet, and e-recording runs through certified partners. Recording a deed costs $45 for page one and $10 for each page after, and your title company normally submits it.

Can I sell a Hillsborough house that has open permits or needs repairs?

Yes, though open permits stay attached to the house. Under the township's rule, whoever owns the property must close an open permit, even one a prior owner pulled. Cash buyers will take a house needing repairs, but resolving the permit first avoids a snag at closing.
